MR. PICKERSGILL    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON JANUARY 27
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising on a question of privilege affecting all hon. members of this house. Your Honour will recall that on Wednesday last I asked the Prime Minister if it was the intention of the government to introduce the necessary measure to allow parliament to express itself about the 50-50 payment to the farmers of western Canada before all the money had been spent. That will be found on page 394 of Hansard.
The Prime Minister, after suggesting that I had not been in the house when this matter came up, went on to say:
-it was made perfectly clear that no action would be taken by the government of Canada until parliament had acted.
The Winnipeg Free Press of Friday, January 29 contains a report from the Manitoba legislature about this exchange, which reads as follows:
Manitoba has a verbal agreement with the federal government to share equally assistance payments to farmers in the province, Hon. George Hutton, minister of agriculture, said Thursday.
He was answering a question from Nelson Shoemaker (Liberal-Gladstone). Mr. Shoemaker asked him to explain "why the Prime Minister in the House of Commons indicated no such undertaking has yet been given."
My point of order is this. Surely an agreement, even if it is a verbal agreement-and I asked the Prime Minister whether there was a verbal agreement, and he gave no answer-was action by the government, and this house was misled by the Prime Minister when he said no action was to be taken until parliament had had an opportunity to debate this matter.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON JANUARY 27
speechtext: The hon. gentleman, whom I heard on the radio yesterday, has just been out in Manitoba engaged in an autopsy on his party. There was no misleading of parliament in any way. The statement which I made is in accordance with the facts.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON JANUARY 27
speechtext: The facts speak for themselves.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce an appointment that I am sure will be of interest to all hon. members of the house. It will be recalled that the distinguished Auditor General, Mr. Watson Sellar, reached the compulsory retirement age since the last session of parliament. I wish now to announce that the government has appointed Mr. Andrew Maxwell Henderson to succeed Mr. Sellar in this important post. His appointment will be effective March 1.

Inquiries of the Ministry
Mr. Henderson is at present the comptroller and chief financial officer of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. He has had a long and successful career in business and in the public service. He qualified as a chartered accountant in Nova Scotia in 1929 and practised this profession in Halifax and later in Toronto until 1935. He was a business executive from 1935 to 1940 and again after the war until his appointment to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in 1957. During the war he served in the foreign exchange control board and as assistant to the chairman and comptroller of the wartime prices and trade board. During 1956 and 1957 he was chairman of the executive council of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to either the Prime Minister or the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and ask if they could confirm or otherwise the shocking report carried over the British Broadcasting Corporation in which it was stated that approximately 150 young student freedom fighters who participated in the Hungarian revolution of 1956 have been executed.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secreiary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in addition to the radio report there was also a dispatch in this morning's Globe and Mail which I have seen. We have as yet no information on which to confirm or reject this report, but the report in itself gives us grounds for renewed concern.
Hon. members will recall that there was a similar report circulating last fall which aroused considerable feeling in Canada and in other western countries. The question was thoroughly discussed during the fourteenth session of the United Nations general assembly last fall. Hon. gentlemen will recall that a resolution dealing with the situation was brought before the assembly co-sponsored by Canada. At that time the Canadian representative, my parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) said that while the Canadian government did not necessarily believe all the rumours that had been circulating he could not deny that these reports had greatly disturbed the Canadian people. He appealed to the Hungarian authorities to allow some neutral investigation of the charges which had been made. He went on to say:
TMr. Diefenbaker.]
We sincerely hope that the alleged events, harmful to the good name of the government of Hungary in its treatment of young offenders, are not taking place as reported throughout the world. But we cannot be content with a silence that may imply damaging admissions. It is for the government of Hungary to move all of us from suspicion to satisfaction, from a sense of distress to a knowledge that puts conscience to rest.
This was the only practical action that Canada could take at that time, and we took it hoping that it might help prevent any further executions taking place. If we are able to get further information of course we will take whatever steps are possible. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) will realize that information on actions of this kind is extremely hard to get and, as I said at the beginning of my reply, we have had no additional information.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. Will the Prime Minister comment on the answer given to the western farm delegation that waited on the government last Saturday, and also with regard to the question of deficiency payments to western farmers?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a group of representatives of western agriculture met with the cabinet on Saturday and made a submission which was delivered by Mr. Wesson and about which several other members made additional representations. The whole question as set out in the terms of the submission received the fullest discussion.
In addition to the general discussion of the subject of deficiency payments, certain representations were, in the view of the government, restated in the nature of alternatives. These questions included the implementation of the two-price system for wheat. Under this proposal wheat sold in Canada for human consumption would be priced at levels related to the level of the domestic economy. I am quoting from the brief; second, provision for payment from the treasury to compensate for the exchange premium on the Canadian dollar; third, acceptance by the government of the responsibility of paying the storage charges on all grain in commercial storage positions; finally, acceptance by the government of the responsibility of subsidizing flour exports. The delegation made its representation in a very frank manner and the entire subject, not

only of deficiency payments as such but the four alternatives to which I have referred, was discussed.
It was pointed out that the view of the government with regard to the question of deficiency payments has not been altered as a result of representations made since that view was expressed in August, 1958. However, with the alternatives before us the delegation was advised that a final decision would be announced in parliament within a period of 30 days. That announcement, of course, will cover not only the whole problem of deficiency payments but as well the several alternatives to which I have made reference.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister whether the representations which were made on this occasion were the same as those made by representatives of the farm unions over a year ago, on which action was promised at that time?

Mr. Speaker, naturally there were further representations; otherwise the representatives of western farm organizations would not have been here. My answer to the hon. gentleman is that in addition to what was stated when the farm delegations were here, further elucidation and enlargement of representations then made and such additional ones as the intervening events made necessary were placed before the cabinet.

I should like to ask a supplementary question arising particularly out of that part of the Prime Minister's statement in which he said that the government has not changed its position since August, 1958. Does this mean that the government is still opposed to deficiency payments, as it was at that time, and that in spite of the presentation that was made on March 10 and the assurance that continued consideration was being given to this problem the government had already given its answer, and the consideration given was very little?

The hon. gentleman, with somewhat usual alacrity, has misinterpreted my remarks. The general view was expressed in August of 1958, and representations were made by a large representative group of western farmers in March. Since then continuous consideration has been given to these representations, now enlarged and expanded as a result of the meeting on Saturday last.

Is the government giving any consideration whatsoever to introducing legislation which would implement its promise of parity prices, something which goes far beyond deficiency payments?

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: BOMAP.C MISSILE  REPORTED SIXTH TEST FAILURE
speechtext: should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. In view of the fact that the Bomarc B interceptor missile is reported to have failed for the sixth straight time at Cape Canaveral on January 29, can the minister state whether the government is going to persist in its plan to spend $125 million to build two Bomarc B bases in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. G. R. Pearkes (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: BOMAP.C MISSILE  REPORTED SIXTH TEST FAILURE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I anticipated that there might be some such question on the Bomarc tests, and over the week end I have been in touch with the secretary of defense of the United States. With the permission of the house I will read a statement which I received from the secretary this morning concerning these tests.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: BOMAP.C MISSILE  REPORTED SIXTH TEST FAILURE
speechtext: Has the minister leave to make this statement?

subtopic: BOMAP.C MISSILE  REPORTED SIXTH TEST FAILURE
speechtext: Agreed.

subtopic: BOMAP.C MISSILE  REPORTED SIXTH TEST FAILURE
speechtext:
Although the latest test of a Bomarc B missile did not result in the successful attainment of all the desired test objectives, the secretary's office today indicated its confidence that the basic missile design is sound. The secretary's office did express concern, however, lest false impressions be created as to the status of the development through lack of proper understanding of the total program and the status of the test program.
It noted that the Bomarc A missile has performed successfully in a large number of tests which have proved the soundness of the missile, its compatability with the SAGE system and its effectiveness against a variety of aerodynamic targets of different sizes and speed characteristics. Operational Bomarc A missiles are now on alert at McGuire air force base in New Jersey and Suffolk, New York.
The development of the B version of the Bomarc was initiated to provide a growth weapon system with double the range of the A version, which would have a greatly improved capability against high speed targets at altitudes down to sea level and which would incorporate various other improvements including the use of a solid propellant booster and a high performance ram jet engine. Early versions of the improved ram jet engine were used in the initial test
79951-0-354
Inquiries of the Ministry flights of the B missile. The solid propellant booster has functioned perfectly in all six tests to date. In the first five flights the ram jet engine failed to perform properly. However, the analysis of the test data revealed deficiencies in the fuel pump and mach control system. These have been corrected, together with other demonstrated weaknesses in the engine system. A successful test of the modified engine on the X-7 ram jet test vehicle two weeks ago provided encouragement that the engine difficulties had been successfully overcome.
In the latest test flight, the sixth in the B series, the solid propellant booster functioned perfectly, the sustainer ram jet engine ignited and performed successfully. Unfortunately a failure in a minor element of the guidance subsystem caused the missile to obtain erroneous attitude information and ultimately to fail in attempting to respond to the wrong data. The ram jet engine, which had been the cause of failure in the first five tests, performed remarkably well and operated successfully well beyond its design performance limits. The component failure in the guidance subsystem is believed to be of a random nature, and reflects in no way on the adequacy of the missile design. This basic subsystem has performed satisfactorily in the case of the A missile and the previous B tests.
Any failure is unfortunate but it is a part of any normal missile development program. The secretary's office indicated its confidence that the Bomarc B weapon system will achieve the potential which will make it a vital element in the air defence system which is being implemented for the defence of the North American continent.
With respect to the last part of the question, there is no intention of making any change in the government's program at the present time, and I do not confirm or deny the figure which was given by the hon. member with respect to the cost.

subtopic: BOMAP.C MISSILE  REPORTED SIXTH TEST FAILURE
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. In view of the latter part of the statement by the Minister of National Defence, will he advise the house as to why it is advisable to go ahead with an expenditure on bases until such time as they know they have a successful project? In view of the statement by the minister concerning the correctness of the design, would he propose that the next test be the shooting up of the design instead of the missile?

subtopic: BOMAP.C MISSILE  REPORTED SIXTH TEST FAILURE
speechtext:
The desirability to proceed with the construction of the bases from which the missile will be fired here in Canada arises so that completion of the site may conform to the date upon which it is expected that the

Inquiries of the Ministry missiles will be delivered to Canada. It is the intention that the sites will be ready when the missiles begin to arrive in Canada during the summer of 1961.
Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the
Opposition): In view of the unimpaired confidence which the minister has stated the Canadian and United States governments have in this weapon, would the minister care to comment on the decision of the United States government to reduce its appropriations this year for that weapon?

subtopic: BOMAP.C MISSILE  REPORTED SIXTH TEST FAILURE
speechtext:
I have no knowledge of a reduction in the appropriations for the coming year. During the last year there was a considerable reduction in the appropriations, because a number of missile sites were removed in the southern part of the United States. They retained the sites on the periphery of the northern boundary of the United States and Canada.
It may interest the hon. member to know that in this year's budget-that is, the coming year's budget-the United States have included $421,500,000 for the Bomarc B project.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the annual meeting of the board of governors of the international bank at Washington last September and October a decision was taken to refer to the executive board of the bank proposals for the
Inquiries of the Ministry formation of an international development association, and to formulate articles of association for the purpose. There was no commitment at that time on the part of any country beyond a decision that the matter should be referred to the executive board for study.

Mr. Speaker, may I add a few words on the contemptible way in which the government, and more particularly the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), dealt with the recommendation of the civil service commission with regard to salary raises for civil servants.
It must be admitted that the Conservative government has made an outward show of dazzling honestly and strictness. Of their own free will, they appointed a special committee within the commission, which was instructed to make certain recommendations to the government. If the cabinet took the trouble to make such appointments, it surely trusted the civil servants who were chosen to this end.
The special investigation committee went thoroughly into the matter and submitted to the Minister of Finance a report recommending an increase. If the government was sincere.-and I hope it was, for once, in appointing those officers-why did it not accept the

On the other hand, if the government was not sincere, or lacked confidence in the officials so appointed, why did it want to create an impression of genuine interest in civil servants?
Anyone who knows what is back of the mind of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) and of the Minister of Finance and of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan), and especially of the former secretary of state who was obliged to resign merely because of delicate health, will scarcely be surprised at the government's disregard for the civil service. Since the government's sole concern is political, and thinks only of being re-elected, we readily understand why it pays little heed to a small minority of faithful public servants, when there are thousands of other voters who might be gained by means of glittering promises. However, the government is showing very bad judgment.
It seems to forget how very lucky it is to be able to rely on civil servants for the administration of the country while the ministers gad about the globe.
The Prime Minister, more particularly noted as a great traveller, and the Minister of Finance, without forgetting the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green), should appreciate the fact that they can rely upon the loyalty and honesty unmatched anywhere else, of the civil servants to see to the good administration of this country, at least when they, the ministers, are gadding about.
Is it not just about the only time that the country can count on intelligent and sincere management with regard to the welfare of Canadian citizens?
By their arrogant behaviour towards the country's best servants, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance have created a feeling of frustration among public employees, and they are destroying the pride that civil servants had in working for the government.
Already, by its irresponsible and unfair behaviour the Conservative government has abetted the resignation of several top-flight officials who might have prevented the government's blunders.
At the same time, the Tories are managing to keep the best qualified Canadians from entering their country's service where they would be useful to their fellow Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to take only a few minutes of the time of the house today for a specific purpose. When I spoke in the debate last week my time ran out just as I was about to start to explain the deficiency payment program for eggs and how it will operate. In view of the confusion which seems to exist in regard to this matter I think it is desirable and important that I should make an explanation to the house with respect to it.
In reporting on the egg situation I think it is important first to state the precise nature of the problem. In simple terms it is that over recent years the production of eggs in Canada has expanded to a point well beyond
[Mr. Loiselle.l
the amount which can be marketed in an orderly way in Canada or in such export markets as are available to us. This has not been a development of the past year; it has accumulated progressively since 1955. In that year 5.6 million cases of eggs were marketed by producers through egg stations. In 1956 the marketings were 6.1 million cases, but the market was able to absorb that quantity without any serious impact on prices.
In each of the next two years marketings were 6.7 million cases, and in 1959 they reached 7.3 million cases. Until October 1, 1959 the market was supported by direct government purchases at the support price. In 1957 the government purchases were 399,940 cases; in 1958, 354,000 cases; in 1959, to the end of September, 936,000 cases. Had purchases by the stabilization board continued throughout all of 1959 the total would have exceeded 1 million cases.
This increasing production has developed in spite of declining egg prices over the last three years. The average price received for eggs by producers in both 1955 and 1956 was 38.1 cents per dozen. In 1957 it was 31.4 cents. There was a minor increase in 1958 to 32.7 cents, but in 1959 the average price dropped to 29.2 cents. The fact is that technological advances in egg production have been such that it was evident that under any reasonable level of support, so long as the stabilization board offered a guaranteed market for any eggs produced the production of eggs, particularly by large commercial operations, would continue to expand. The government, therefore, reached the decision that it was necessary to discontinue supporting the market by purchasing eggs. In place of that a deficiency payment program was established.
While it was obviously desirable to discontinue the system under which the government was accumulating eggs in an unmanageable volume, of even greater importance in the interests of the industry itself was the necessity of cutting production back to more realistic proportions. In establishing the deficiency payment arrangement it was provided that producers would be eligible for up to 4,000 dozen grade A large eggs a year. This represents the production of a flock of about 500 laying hens. The establishment of this maximum brought charges from the more commercialized side of the poultry industry that the government was subsidizing inefficient production and holding back technological improvements. I think it is obvious that this is an unfair charge to lay against a department which devotes as much attention to research, to the improvement and efficiency of production, as does the Department of Agriculture.

The fact is, however, that the increase in production which has led to the present problem has come largely from the growth in highly commercialized egg operations. To continue to provide full support to them could only negate one of the main objectives of the deficiency payment program. This program is deliberately designed to protect the average farm producer against the impact of lower prices while the necessary adjustment in egg production is taking place.
The house will be interested in some figures on the registration of egg producers for deficiency payments. As of some 10 days or two weeks ago-I got these figures, of course, for a week ago-70,484 producers had registered. Of this number, 90 per cent have 500 birds or less and their entire production of grade A large eggs should be eligible for any deficiency payments which are made.

This historical price performance illustrates that neither a uniform support price throughout Canada nor regional levels supported by purchases by the board have prevented a pattern of comparative average prices between areas based purely on market considerations.
From this background the use of national averages, both for the support level and in determining the producer price, was considered to be the only sound basis for fixing the amount of any deficiency payment. It permits the normal, free play of prices between areas and makes it incumbent on those in each area, as I believe it should, to secure the best price available for eggs in Canada or outside the country.
It must be recognized that the egg market at present is going through a difficult period while an adjustment is being made to more realistic production levels. It requires only a relatively small reduction in laying flocks to achieve that purpose. There are indications of some increased marketings of laying hens. It is already evident that new hatches this season for future laying flocks will be lighter. Production should be more in line with demand within a few months, and at that time the industry will be in a much sounder position and should be able to look forward to better prices than have prevailed in recent years. In the meantime, during this transition period the deficiency payments will ensure that the average total returns received by the great majority of individual producers will be equal to the support price.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I think there is no question but that the matter of a deficiency payment program of this kind is a somewhat complex matter, and there is considerable difficulty in people grasping how it will work, its implications and so forth. I think perhaps these things could be made much clearer by a concrete example on the basis of what the prices have been during the first three weeks of January, for which of course we now have the figures, in order to illustrate how the deficiency payment system would work as far as that three-week period is concerned.
Up to this time we have really had no definite figures upon which one could quote concrete examples. The national weighted average support price is, of course, 33 cents a dozen. The cumulative weighted average price which producers received for the first three weeks of January was 19.3 cents.

speechtext: That is grade A large?

speechtext:
Yes, this is all grade A large. In other words, during the first three weeks of January the weighted average price producers received for their eggs was 19.3 cents. Thus, if a deficiency payment were

made at the present time for that first three-week period in January, the payment would be 13.7 cents a dozen. That is to say, as at the end of the third week of January the producers of eggs in this country had owing to them a deficiency payment of 13.7 cents a dozen.
Of course if the price for eggs goes lower than it was during the first three weeks of January, and remains lower throughout the remaining period of January, February and March, then the deficiency payment will be more than 13.7 cents. If the price of eggs goes up during February and March, then the deficiency payment will be less than the 13.7 cents. But in any event the price the producer receives will be brought up on the average of his return to 33 cents a dozen, which is the support price.
Of course this does not mean that each individual producer in any area will get 33 cents. The amount he gets depends on what he sold his eggs for to begin with, and the normal sort of differentials which have always existed in the past between the prices of eggs in one part of the country compared with another would operate. If one looks at egg prices at the present time one will see there is quite a range of prices which producers are receiving, going from Newfoundland to British Columbia.
The situation in regard to the use of regional average prices rather than a national average price can, I think, also be shown very well on the basis of prices during this first three-week period of January, as well as showing what the situation would be if a deficiency payment were being made for these three weeks only. If we had a regional support price in Manitoba instead of the national average support price-and this is what has been asked for by some of the egg producers in Manitoba, and also Saskatchewan-the regional support price would not be 33 cents but 27.7 cents, which of course is the average of the prices received there over the past ten years, which has always been lower than the average price in Ontario and Quebec. The regional support price in Manitoba, if it were on a regional basis, would be 27.7 cents. The average price received by producers in the first three weeks of January, as far as Manitoba is concerned, was 15.2 cents. Therefore the deficiency payment they would receive for this three-week period would be 12.5 cents, which is of course 1.2 cents a dozen less than they would receive by using a national average. Therefore, as far as that three-week period is concerned, the producers in Manitoba are better off under a national

average than under a regional average, and I think the same would apply throughout any particular year.
On a national average return in Saskatchewan, without going into the figures and taking up the time of the house, the return to the producers for the first three weeks in January would have been 1.3 cents a dozen more than if we had used a regional average.
In Alberta, as it happens, there is a somewhat different situation. On a national average basis the return would be .2 cents below the return on a regional basis for those three weeks. But taking the situation over any year I think there is no question but that the use of a national average is a much fairer and better method than the use of regional averages. Also, as far as the western provinces are concerned, I think they would be better off under that system than they would be under the use of regional averages.
The deficiency payment method of support for hogs will work in much the same way as I outlined a deficiency payment method for eggs would work. It will ensure that the great bulk of our producers will receive on the average the support price of $22.65 a hundred during 1959. We believe that the deficiency payment method of support for eggs and hogs on a limited amount of production will provide to the great bulk of our producers the minimum prices which they require, and at the same time will bring production down into line with what can be marketed. When that situation has been realized, egg and hog prices should reach satisfactory levels for our producers; and this, of course, is the ultimate aim of our deficiency payment programs.

The Address-Mr. heduc
Last fall, a noteworthy event took place in my constituency. I refer to the official opening of the first section of the Gatineau parkway. In fact in October last, the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Diefenbaker) officially opened that first section of the parkway, which one day will extend throughout Gatineau park. It is a marvellous parkway, leading from Gamelin boulevard in Hull to a distance of twelve miles into the Gatineau hills. That project, initiated a few years ago, has now been completed by the government.
The house undoubtedly knows that the Gatineau park development project is part of the national capital development project. I am sure the house will want that project to be completed as soon as possible. I am also convinced that the government realizes the importance of the project and that it will complete the development of that park as soon as the country's financial situation permits.
I should like also to call the attention of the house to an important announcement made last fall, when the government accepted the recommendations of the national capital commission with regard to the removal of Union station and the railway tracks to a point a few miles away from the capital, that is, beyond the Rideau river in the vicinity of Hurdman's bridge.
This is a wise policy on the part of the government and I should like to commend it for that because, in the N.C.C. report, where reference is made to railway tracks, Mr. Greber states that the removal of Union station and of the railway tracks from the centre of the national capital is the key to the whole national capital development project. It is not necessary to be an expert town-planner to know that in removing the station and the railway tracks from the centre of the capital, traffic conditions will, at the same time, be improved. After the railway tracks are removed, the city of Ottawa and the national capital commission will be able to build driveways, new roads and new streets on the present site of those tracks relieving congestion in that area and, at the same time, taking care of the traffic problem in the downtown area.
The project will be of benefit not only to the city of Ottawa but also to the city of Hull, because important railway sections will be eliminated, a new railway station will be built and railway tracks on the interprovincial bridge will also disappear. This will help in no 

small way to solve the traffic problem in the city of Hull and even to beautify this city.
I do not want to miss this opportunity to say a few words about the building of a new bridge between Ottawa and Hull. A new bridge is all the more urgent because it would not only serve Ottawa and Hull, but also my own riding, as well the Papineau and Labelle ridings, and finally all the northern ridings such as Abitibi county, whose people must cross one of those bridges when they come to Ottawa.
I know that the government favours the building of a new bridge and I hope that an agreement can be reached with the authorities, either provincial or municipal, so that this bridge may be built soon.
The other day I read with interest the speech delivered by the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau). I was particularly interested in the part of his speech dealing with the deepening of the Ottawa river.
This matter is of great importance for the industrial development of my constituency and area. The chambers of commerce, that is to say the western Quebec union of chambers of commerce, have asked the government to consider the scheme, and today I only wish to renew their representations and ask the government to give serious and thorough consideration to the matter.
The matter of deepening the Ottawa river is a highly important matter. If, after giving it serious study, the government reaches the conclusion that the scheme would not be economic, I would ask them not to undertake it, because we already have enough costly programs to support or, to use a popular expression, the government has enough white elephants on its hands without taking up another one. But I should like to point out that the situation of the Ottawa and Hull area, for the last few years, has substantially changed from the point of view of industrial development. Several of those industries in the area are kept going or have developed, thanks to the natural resources of my constituency and of those of neighbouring constituencies I refer to forests.
Several mills produce hundreds of tons of newsprint daily, and those products are exported abroad especially to the American market, but also to European markets.
Those are basic industries in the area. They have been there for generations. For, if we

The Address-Mr. Leduc
know how to take care of the development of our forests, those industries will be kept going indefinitely.
But there are not only wood products and by-products to be exported from that area. There are also the products of the mines. Various mines have been developed lately in the district, more particularly the Hull iron mine where iron ore is extracted. That mine is now in full operation and its iron ore will have to be sent either into the province of Quebec or to other parts of Canada, if not to other countries abroad.
It is therefore important that low cost transport facilities be available to those new mines. There is also in my constituency an important mine operated by the Aluminum Company of Canada, the Farm Point mine which produces lime and magnesium oxide. That mine operates the year round and is bound to expand with the development of Canada and especially with the expansion of foreign markets, provided they are accessible to it. For that reason, transport rates are an important factor in the success of that concern.
There are also in the Lievre region considerable asbestos deposits which could be developed. There again, if transport facilities were provided, and especially if the costs of transportation were reasonable, those deposits could be developed. Therefore, I hope that the government will take into serious consideration the possibility of deepening the Ottawa river. And as I said a moment ago, if following such a study it proves to be profitable for the region and the country to undertake this work, I shall most certainly support the government in the implementation of this project.

Mr. Speaker, I said a moment ago that I was not going to read such a long list of loans, but I should like to establish a comparison between loans granted to a nearby municipality, the municipality of Buckingham. I have here a copy of the newspaper Le Droit of December 17, 1959, in which we read that the Buckingham school board had floated debentures to an amount of $346,000; they were sold last December at an interest rate of 7.727 per cent. In the same article, it is said that in December 1955, the same board had sold bends for a total of $755,000 at 3 J and 4 per cent, that is a 15 year series at the price of 97.69, or a net cost of 4.165 per cent.
That goes to prove, Mr. Speaker, that interest rates went up considerably these last few years and it is precisely the interest rate which at the present time concerns provincial and municipal governments as well as school boards.
I could give many examples. I could tell of a particular case where a school board in my constituency sold debentures last August for the construction of a sixteen room school. The board needed $321,000. An architect was asked to draw up the plans. The board invited tenders, and last August let the contract for the construction of the school. But when the board went to the bank for a loan to finance the construction pending the sale of debentures, the bank flatly refused. That is when the school board approached the municipal affairs commission of Quebec because the school board did not want to sell its debentures last September, since the bond market was too unfavourable. Well, the official of the municipal affairs commission of Quebec could only suggest to the school board to wait until March or April of 1960 to place its debentures on the bond market.
Mr. Speaker, the debentures were not sold and the building is not going up because the school board does not have the money to finance the project.
That is the type of situation which is causing concern among the population, and not only the public organizations, but individuals and businessmen too. Businessmen and small tradesmen who have to borrow money today have a real hard time to find a lender, especially one who would be ready to loan money at reasonable rates. I know people who have paid 7, 8, 9 or 10 per cent interest on a well secured first mortgage loan.

Mr. Speaker, that money is hard to come by. I have read some remarks made by the governor of the Bank of Canada in a speech he made at Winnipeg; and with your permission, 1 should like to quote just one excerpt from that speech, which appeared in the Gazette of Wednesday, January 20, 1960. Mr. Coyne is reported to have made the following statement:
(Text):
Mr. Coyne devoted most of his time and attention to Canada's balance of payments position. And he made it clear that he was alarmed, even horrified, by the prospects of a deficit which will be about as large as the $1.3 billion figure chalked up in 1956 and repeated in 1957.
This sort of thing, he said sharply, might be all very well for a poor, underdeveloped country living "close to the poverty level" and trying desperately to raise living standards in a hurry. But a rich, proud country like Canada? Unthinkable, said Mr. Coyne.
-he said, "We have for at least five years been living beyond our means on a grand scale. Perhaps we have comforted ourselves with the thought that we were by this means increasing from year to year the total productive capacity of the Canadian economy by a sufficient extra margin to enable us before long to balance our foreign accounts, live within our expanding means and even at some time begin to pay off our foreign debt. But this has not happened. Exports are rising but imports are rising faster. We are not producing ourselves out of our import deficit but are getting in deeper."
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, the governor of the Bank of Canada suggested to his listeners that the remedy consisted in living within their means. It is all very well to tell us to live within our means, but it seems to me that the government should start by setting the example. Now, if we are having monetary difficulties at present, it is precisely because of the government's monetary policy.
The country has been living beyond its means and the government since coming into power has spent much more than it could afford. Since the government came into power shortages have been piling up and, to make up those shortages, the government has to borrow money. The federal government is monopolizing the money supply, and that is the chief reason why provincial governments, city councils and school boards can no longer borrow, at reasonable rates, the money they need to finance worthwhile projects.
Through its trade policy, the government has also put the country in a serious predicament. During the election campaign, the government denounced our trade imbalance with other countries. What is the situation today? The government was supposed to solve this problem by diverting to European

countries our trade with the United States. The situation today is that our exports show a deficit of more than $1,300 million and, to make up for this deficit, the government has to spend its own money.
The government monetary policy results in deficits, therefore, the government should adopt, at least today, a policy designed to reduce to some extent the value or the premium of the Canadian dollar. At present, the 5 per cent premium-that is, the 5 per cent difference between the Canadian dollar and the American dollar-constitutes an export tariff equal to the difference in value between the Canadian dollar and the American dollar.
Such tariff places our exporters at a disadvantage; and that has considerably affected the export of our products.
We all know that Canada is a country which produces much more than it can consume, since it has to export at least 75 per cent of its production. Well, in order to be able to export those products, a foreign market is absolutely necessary. To find a foreign market, Canadian products must necessarily be in a position to compete with those of other countries on world markets. Now, I said that the high rate of interest on money helps increase not only the cost of living but the cost of products we have to consume here and that we should be exporting.
I would ask the government, which has competent economists at its disposal in the field of financial administration, to gather those people together, to take their advice, and thus be in a position to give the country a policy which will save us from disaster. Because we are now headed for ruin, and if the government does not take the necessary steps as soon as possible we shall run into disaster.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have this somewhat belated opportunity to extend my congratulations to you upon your selection to the post which you occupy. Those of us who knew you realized that you possessed the ability required for this position and you have, I have noted, had some opportunity during the course of the last week or ten days to display this talent and to indicate that the choice was an excellent one.
The Address-Mr. Baldwin
I should like also to congratulate the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Morissette) and the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman) who were respectively the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I feel that this was a most excellent choice, the blending of the scholarly and informative tone of the mover of the address with the wit, wisdom and human touch of the seconder. This showed that the choice was well made. I should like to say also although I have not the flair of my colleagues from the province of Quebec for this sort of thing, that it is a pleasure for us to have a member who is as pleasing to the eye as she is to the ear.
I listened with interest to the comments and observations of the opposition speakers in this debate. I want to make some comments with regard to the contributions made by hon. members from the official opposition. It is rather difficult at this stage of the debate because, in the first place, I do not think they have made too many points that merit any reply; and second, by this late date most of the speakers from the government side have dealt more than adequately with what the opposition speakers have had to say.
However, there is one fundamental weakness which I suggest appears in the type of criticism the opposition speakers have had to offer, what I would call the "yes, but" treatment. They very transparently give lip service to some legislation or some principle which they are not too happy about but which they are afraid to oppose. Therefore they say there is something wrong with it; that this is wrong or that is wrong, and then they detail a long, tedious and minor list of complaints not very relevant.
I think an example of that is the treatment accorded to the farm legislation recently enacted in connection with assistance to certain distressed areas in western Canada. It was true enough that the hon. members ended up by voting for these bills, but I felt from where I sat that they did so with reluctance and dislike, and were in fact dragged kicking and screaming to record their approval. I would suggest that in my opinion, if events had transpired differently on March 31, 1958 and, unfortunately for this country, the members sitting in the official opposition had formed the government, there would have been no legislation to provide assistance to the farmers of western Canada.
So far as the C.C.F. group is concerned, one distinct impression is obtained. The remarks of their party bring home to a listener a
566	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Baldwin phenomenon apparent in so many western countries, namely the intellectual and policymaking bankruptcy and physical collapse of the socialist parties. In saying this I do so without in any way intending not to give full credit to the achievements of this party under their leaders in the last three or four decades, but I think we have to remember that this was a movement that arose and grew during, and probably because of, a transition in human progress and development; that is to say, the merging of the sharp lines of distinction in society to a larger, more homogeneous group with barely perceptible lines of distinction either socially or economically. The very fact that this has occurred at all, and that it occurred under the aegis and stimulus of our system of individual incentive, which is a proposition the socialists said was utterly impossible, has consequently branded them as false prophets and has destroyed the very pith and substance and the heart and soul of their movement.
I do not intend to suggest that this withering away of class lines and the general improvement in the welfare of the people has yet run its course, though certainly under the administration of the late Liberal government it was grinding to a halt. There is still much to do, and undoubtedly since June 1957 great progress has been made along those lines.
In this regard it is of interest to examine certain remarks made by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), who in this debate took the opportunity to reiterate his indictment of our system of life. True enough, Mr. Speaker, it would be a very brave or foolish person who would suggest that all was for the best in the best of all possible worlds. Ours is a system of trial and error, and inevitably there will be mistakes and errors, some injustices and some inequities. As a matter of fact, when any amendment or act of parliament is passed it is an admission that there is prima facie, a defect in the existing law which needed to be attended to, or that an improvement required to be made.
But how much worse would the people and economy of this country have been if they had been held tight by the doctrinaire rigidity and strait-jacket control of our socialist friends. In any event, I think the hon. members of the C.C.F. party have come face to face with the facts of life about their continued existence. They realize that they are probably coming apart at the seams. All one has to do is read the newspapers and see what is happening in the United Kingdom. When you hear of the convulsions, the rumblings and the dissensions in the Labour party of the United Kingdom you realize exactly what is happening.


For this reason these knights in shining armour, probably like the Chevalier Bayard, "sans peur et sans reproche", but most certainly "sans program" and "sans future", are striving in every way to find a new policy which they hope will permit them to move over a little further to the left and replace the official opposition. Their method is obviously to say something about everything. The reflection of this is shown in the great list of resolutions, questions and bills which appears on the order paper of this house under their names, all in search of some popular cause which they hope will halt the decline and fall of the C.C.F. party.
As a private member I regard with some apprehension the deluge of words which will descend upon our heads during the course of this present session. In my innocence, Mr. Speaker, I would have thought that at the conclusion of the last session there would not have been one single member of the C.C.F. party who had an unuttered thought left about a single matter. It appears I was wrong. In any event, the measure of their desperation is shown by the fact that the variety and multiplicity of the subject matters they are dealing with is equalled only by the shallowness of the treatment they are according them.
There are two exerpts from the speech from the throne about which I would like to comment; in fact I shall direct the rest of my remarks to them. I think they should probably be taken out of context and read together. The first extract appears on page 2 of Hansard for January 14, and is as follows:
Economic and technical assistance to the less developed nations of the world continues to be needed both on humanitarian grounds and to provide the economic basis for peaceful and orderly progress in those nations.
The second quotation is a little further on:
The growing exports of various countries are presenting us with both increasing opportunities for trade and problems of competition.
May I say that I would like to see something more of an air of urgency, with apt words setting this out to describe this situation. I think the urgency of the first proposal can best be illustrated by paraphrasing what was said by a great United States president:
This world will not long endure with the majority of its inhabitants barely existing on starvation rations and the rest more than well fed.
To this end the economic and technical assistance which has been mentioned is of the most vital importance to the future peace and security of the world. But for this to be so I think we must keep steadily and clearly before us the fact that alms are distasteful, and that nobody likes relief. I hope

it will be accepted and stated in suitable language that what we expend now, as well as in the future, is not in such a category but is instead what might properly be called an investment in our friends and neighbours; those who are now, and who we hope will in the future, be our business associates and trading partners.
To keep in perspective what this might mean to us at a later date I want to refer again to the second statement from the speech from the throne:
The growing exports of various countries are presenting us with both increasing opportunities for trade and problems of competition.
I would remind you that "the growing exports of various countries" referred to in the extract are to a great extent exports from countries many of which a few short years ago lay exhausted by the extraordinary demands and effects of a great world war. These nations showed themselves capable of a remarkable recovery. True enough they had the assistance of the Marshall plan; they were in the happy position that they were able to replace the plant which had been bombed and destroyed with a plant which was new in its entirety.
That, of course, has been a tremendous advantage to them; but I would suggest there is surely no doubt that they have shown themselves capable of a tremendous recovery, and we must anticipate that in the same way the fierce, explosive forces which have led to the political emancipation of so many new nations already formed, and so many others now struggling to be born in Africa and Asia, must in a similar way lead in a very short time-a period much shorter than any of us contemplated-to a rapid and tremendous expansion of economic growth in those countries. I suggest that this economic expansion may in turn produce a tremendous surge of consumer demand which might well prove to be the great motivating factor in these countries over the next quarter century.
I perused a thoughtful and provocative article in the Christian Science Monitor a few days ago which suggested that the increasing awareness and pressure of consumer requirements in all the communist countries could be one of the most potent factors in compelling an acceptable form of coexistence. While I recommend this article to the house for consideration and examination, it is only with qualifications because this is an oversimplification of a very complex problem.
It would be foolish for us at this time, even believing this to some extent, to drop our guard or relax our defence. It would be equally futile not to recognize that we must expect, in the immediate future, a savage measure of economic competition from those
The Address-Mr. Baldwin communist countries. Nevertheless, as an increasingly large number of their people become exposed to the mellowing influences of a better standard of living we can expect that this, more than anything else, will enable something to be worked out, if for no other reason than that the alternative is probably too appalling. Thus the challenge will be not only to meet new competition, but also to meet the insatiable demand of the many hundreds of millions of people in this world for the goods and services which increased trade would provide for them, and a better way of life.
We must, however, take care that in trying to meet this demand we do not place any formidable obstructions in the way of free trading relations between nations.
The extent to which we in Canada can meet this potential challenge will be determined by the prudent and careful mobilization and use of our resources, and in this regard the wisdom of the present policy of national resource development initiated by this government is to be highly commended. There are many facets to this problem, and many areas are affected, but I naturally prefer to view it in the light of its application to the northwest part of Canada because I come from there, I know the area and I realize that it contains a reservoir of many of those commodities which the world will require before too many years have passed; also, I think, because it reflects the famous complaint of Cecil Rhodes-"so much to do, so little time".
I would emphasize that the particular district I have in mind is not necessarily restricted to my own constituency. As a matter of fact it probably embraces parts of four or five constituencies. It includes all that part of Canada lying west of the pre-Cambrian shield, east of the Rocky mountains, north of the 55th parallel of north latitude and extending to, and including, parts of the Great Slave lake area, a region containing some 200,000 square miles of territory.
This is a natural economic and geographic unit containing a substantial list of resources which grows in kind and in quantity with each inventory that is made. For example, the natural gas discoveries made in those portions of the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia and in the Northwest Territories suggest beyond any doubt that this area contains what may well be the largest reserves of natural gas on the North American continent. I have heard figures given by experts, not without substantial confirmation in so far as lumber and pulp are concerned, showing that the potential of the area is probably at least 200 million board feet a year and that it may well be as much as

The Address-Mr. Baldwin 300 million board feet, with pulpwood for at least three mills plus another at the city of Grande Prairie, plans for which are now reaching fruition, and others depending on the quality of the timber which will be available when steps are taken for the construction of the reservoir for the Peace river dam.
The waterpower to be developed on this great river at Hudson Hope canyon is rated at about five million horsepower upstream benefit. I pause here to suggest to those responsible for the negotiations for the development of additional sources of power in the west that nothing should be done which would improperly or unduly delay or prejudice this great scheme. I say this holding no brief for any group or organization which is concerned with this power development.
I think the interests of this country will be served by the integrated development of more than one source of power. Recently I read reports in the United States press of a meeting of the American association of mining and metallurgical engineers in San Francisco. At that meeting a number of papers were read by experts who met to discuss the situation with regard to the Paley report which, as hon. members know, was a report to the president of the United States with regard to materiel on the North American continent. These learned authorities concluded that so far as natural gas and electrical energy are concerned the Paley report had underestimated consumption and overestimated the resources which could be developed. In the result we are at the present time a considerable distance behind the timetable envisaged in the Paley report.
I would also commend to the government's attention the excellent analysis made by Dr. John Davis with regard to the suitability and the probability of developing the production of enriched uranium in Canada which pointed naturally to the fact that in his opinion this great source of waterpower, the Peace river, is one of the logical and potential areas where this development could take place.
With regard to agriculture, figures recently have been released following a helicopter survey conducted by the Alberta government. There is one small district alone in the northern part of my constituency where, before the figures were released, it was generally estimated that there were 300,000 acres of arable land available for development. Today, following that report, it has been established that there are over two million acres. This is not land that is going to be placed in wheat production. This is land capable of producing the forage crops, the grasses; broom grass, fescue and alfalfa. All these are products which are and will be required in our economy.


In that regard I am very happy at this time to pay tribute to the excellent way in which the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort has consistently advocated the cause of the rape-seed growers in this country. It may be that in moving around, by a process of intellectual osmosis we pick up some of the better points of our neighbours. In any event I am happy to endorse and confirm what he has said on previous occasions about this commodity.
I have some figures which I will offer to the house and which in my opinion are quite significant. I will offer an analysis of the information I have obtained. We have in a few short years become the world's largest exporter of rapeseed. According to the 1958 statistics, taken from a circular of the United States department of agriculture dealing with world exports of fats and oils dated October 8, 1959, we have, within a decade, come to a position where we now export twice as much rapeseed as any other country in the world.
The importance of this lies in the fact that there are tremendous markets still available all over the world. The very timely article which my genial friend read this morning was a clipping from the Saskatoon Star Phoenix of last Wednesday which indicates that the French government is contemplating sending a mission to Canada to make certain enquiries. It is significant to remember that France was, after us, the second largest exporter of rapeseed.
It has been estimated by competent officials in the Department of Trade and Commerce-and I have taken some steps to confirm this-that we might in due course be able to put into production of rapeseed a total ranging between 1 million to 1J million acres. That will immediately take out of the production of wheat, a commodity which will be in surplus for some years, and place into the production of rapeseed, a commodity for which we have a market, a considerable number of acres. It could mean that we would have between $25 million and $35 million poured into the pockets of farmers at a most timely period during the farm year. For that reason I would commend to the government that it give very serious consideration to trying to replace the production of wheat with the production of rapeseed in appropriate areas.
As I said before, these resources exist. The problem is to work out without delay an acceptable and realistic method to make the best use of them. One needs only to survey the world population situation, in respect of which we are told that in 40 years the total will double to almost 6 billions, to appreciate the need for far-sighted planning. Take, for

instance, the United States, popularly regarded as one of the "have" nations, whose only problem with regard to agriculture appears to be the disposal of its high surplus. Yet there are interesting figures given in pamphlets and papers of the United States department of agriculture which contain projections of population and agricultural production from 1955 to 1975 and which suggest that at the conclusion of 1975, in order to keep pace with a normal increase in population, the United States alone will require agricultural production from 150 million additional acres of new agricultural land but they can see their way clear to actually bringing only approximately 25 million acres into production. That leaves them in the position where they will be required to find additional production by means of technological advances and scientific improvements in their agricultural industry.
Apropos of that I should say it has been brought to my attention that in the United States alone, one million acres each year are taken out of agricultural production as a result of the growth of cities and their suburbs. It is a truism to say that some of the most fertile agricultural land in the North American continent is in close proximity to the cities which usually grow up near that land. The land being taken out of production is, therefore, some of the best producing land on the continent. I suggest that while we have today what appears to be overproduction, this is a situation which may not be of too long duration.
This is the second of the two anomalies which beset and perplex the free governments of the west. First there is the attempt to balance on the razor edge between recession and inflation. Despite the lengthy statements we have heard from hon. members of the opposition with respect to the present situation I am confident from what I have heard and seen that this country has accepted the program of the Minister of Finance in his efforts to find a solution to this problem.
Second, there is the moral as well as the financial problem posed by our having too much in a world where many people have too little, not because they do not want more but because they cannot buy it. I am firmly convinced that finding the right answer to this conundrum is of the greatest consequence. Within the limits of fiscal ability in Canada, our duty as well as self interest must compel us to expand and gear up our national production plant to a point somewhat beyond what appears to be our capacity to absorb or to dispose of through normal commercial channels. We are in a unique position to do this, with a strong and stable industrial economy and a
The Address-Mr. Baldwin vast underdeveloped area waiting to be wakened and brought to life. But if we are to take advantage of the situation labour, industry, capital and government must work together in the closest harmony. Sacrifices must be made, risks accepted and rewards shared to an extent greater than what is presently acceptable if we are to take this tide in our affairs at the flood.
To conclude, I wish to list what I believe are some of the fundamental problems and issues and desirable solutions in connection with northern and national development. In the first instance the development of our resources must primarily and fundamentally be for the benefit of the people, on the simple basis, that the ultimate objective of any scheme of development must be for the benefit of mankind as a whole.
If Canada's progress is to continue evenly the time has now come when we must devote some attention to the problem of the decentralization of population and industry, not by interfering with existing establishments but by reasonable attempts to direct new immigration and even people who are native Canadians into these outlying areas. It seems to me we are too young a country to have already developed that middle aged spread which results from the undue concentration of people and industries into too small an area so that before too many years have passed we will find our problem of transportation, amongst others, will be increased accordingly and compounded. I think we are too virile a nation to accept as our motto, "Life, liberty and the pursuit of indolence". To avoid this, we must pursue our own course and our own destiny of national development and not become a pale and anaemic replica of our great neighbour to the south, and I say that without in any way disparaging that great country.
Our method of development must be such as to create opportunity for the ordinary man and our young people so that they will have access to the natural resources, to settle and establish themselves. It is not good enough to permit those great resources to be developed and exploited by a few greedy, grasping corporations and people. I saw something of this issue during the course of the summer when I appeared before the royal commission inquiring into the railway to the north. This commission is still sitting and, of course, the main issue is sub judice. But, I think, on a collateral issue I am entitled to say that I was shocked to find that here were the railway companies, large corporations, and the mining industry combined to advocate a measure of development which so far as I could see definitely had no place in it for the smaller individual. If there is to be an

The Address-Mr. Baldwin unearned increment resulting from the development of great public works at public expense it is essential that that unearned increment should be to the advantage of the many.
Apropos of this, I suggest that many of these resources, of which I have spoken, particularly minerals, are non-recurrent resources in the nature of capital assets, and it is the duty of the generation which does the development today to do so by a plan which, wherever possible, replaces the assets in the area from which they have taken them with people, with settlement and with industry. Anything less than this can only result in distortion, in a further accentuation of that present distortion in our national growth and economy of which I have already spoken.
The hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Maloney), who made a very good contribution to this debate, dealt with the question of immigration and related it to the development of the northwest of Canada. There is indeed a most valid connotation between these thoughts. The whole broad picture of North American settlement consists of a series of moves from settled east to the open west, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, each move based on periods of intensive immigration combined, of course, with the natural movement of population resulting from industrial dislocation and both movements aided by the spirit of adventure and the desire of people to have access to new country. This no longer necessarily holds true today. The establishment of social justice at its present level, the slowing of immigration, and the dulling of the spirit of adventure, have sensibly diminished almost to a trickle the number of people who are strained through the industrial east and the few large centres west of the great lakes to the north country. Most of those who do come are civil servants and those who do not intend to make a permanent home there and do not make any permanent contribution to the country.
In 1929 and 1933 I was privileged to see what I believe to be the last great immigration of people in the old tradition, when thousands of people came to the Peace river country to found a new life in the country. They came by all kinds of vehicles to the extremities of the frontier. They went by rivers hundreds of miles to found new homes for themselves. These people, in the pattern of which I have seen so much, were people who came before, preceding rather than following the amenities of civilization, the roads, the telegraph lines, the utilities and schools, all these things to which we have become accustomed. I fear that we shall not see the like again; and if we intend to speed up and accelerate the program of national develop-


ment in a true sense, then it is time for us to translate into action measures to try and eliminate the disparities in the standards of living.
Finally, I think that we have now arrived in this country at the point where problems of development in areas where there is divided jurisdiction should be treated in a different manner than formerly. If you take the country I mentioned before, you find the jurisdiction divided between three agencies, namely the government of Canada as represented by the Northwest Territories council, the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, the government of Alberta and the government of British Columbia. As a result there has been in the past a failure to integrate development which has proceeded too often by fits and starts, by stops and reverses. There has been no opportunity to take an over-all, comprehensive bird's eye view of the problems which must be dealt with. Too often people of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources cannot see anything south of the 60th parallel; too often the provincial governments of Alberta and British Columbia have been unable to integrate their schemes of development.
As I said before, the country is an integral unit, an economic and geographic unit, and its progress and development have been hampered-
