Yes, of the other party. I agree with the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Houck) that this debate should be shortened and the length of speeches reduced. It is a fact that any subject mentioned in the speech from the throne will be the subject of discussion when legislation is introduced at a later date and I think that members will have sufficient time to deal with specific matters then. But since it is the practice for everyone at this time to be an expert on all subjects I will not deviate from the rules of the House of Commons.
The speech from the throne, Mr. Speaker, was delivered in two stages, one delivered by His Excellency the Governor General and the other a little later through announcements by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker). In both cases matters were left out which are most important, namely unemployment, defence, monetary policy and social legislation.
I do not want to deal at length with the problems of trade and unemployment because they have been discussed by many speakers. I want to say, however, that our trade situation needs to be overhauled. We should consider seriously the formation of a free trade area in North America and the West Indies. Too many of our tariffs operate against Canadian consumers. We cannot long stand enormous deficits such as we have had in the past year and we must do something to meet the threat of the European common market and Russian trade ascendancy.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Do you mean free trade with the United States?
There is a difference between totally free trade and a free trade agreement with the United States.
Explain.

I do not pose as an expert but I will give an example where our tariffs do not work very well. We have an automobile tariff in this country which is used by United States companies as
The Address-Mr. J. T. Richard an excuse to sell cars made in Canada at a price which includes the tariff and the sales tax.
How would a free trade agreement solve that?
Does the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) agree with you?
Explain what you mean.
The same manufacturers would make the cars here and sell them at the same price as they are sold for in the United States.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Has the hon. member cleared his views with the hon. member for Essex East?

I am speaking for myself and on this side of the house I think I am entitled to have my own opinions on several matters. Like hon. members who were on the other side of the house some years ago, I express my own opinions on certain subjects in an individual way.
Our exports are dependent at the present time to a great extent on the shipment of uranium, lumber and wheat, and already we know that in a few years our uranium shipments could decline very greatly and that we will suffer from aggressive competition by Russia in the wheat and lumber markets. We have priced ourselves out of world markets and have consequently imposed on our own citizens prices which they cannot bear.
The man who is squeezed is the little man, the small businessman and the low wage earner. The cost of living has gone up steadily and his profits or wages are not keeping up to the same level. There are hundreds of thousands of people in this country who are not protected by union agreements, who have no security and no one to defend them. While I am quite in agreement that we should do all we can to help people who are suffering in other parts of the world, I think the time has come to look closely into the problems of our own underprivileged classes in Canada. These people are also suffering from the tight money policy. They are the ones who pay the high interest rates to loan companies and the high prices for merchandise on credit. They are the people who have no money to make a cash deposit on a home. They are the people who are in need of more welfare assistance including a fully comprehensive health insurance plan.
We heard an announcement last Monday, Mr. Speaker, that a committee on defence will sit during the present session. I trust that this committee will discuss the policy as well as the plans which our country has for the defence of Canada. At the present

The Address-Mr. J. T. Richard time it is fair to state that we have no policy. We have a very well trained group of men and women in our armed forces but they are disarmed. They have no weapons, whether missiles, ships or planes, to wage a modern war or to defend against modern war. The government is building Bomarc bases when it is doubtful that the Bomarc will ever be used. The F-104G will not be available for some years to come and by that time may be much more obsolete than the Arrow would have been. As far as our navy is concerned, there is only the promise that we will train some of our men on a borrowed submarine. We have no choice other than to disarm at the present time and to be in favour of disarmament. No wonder we are taking the lead in this regard. In the meantime we must rely entirely on the decision of the people of the United States to defend their country on Canadian soil. There is very little comfort for those civilians who might be caught in a surprise attack because our civil defence is disorganized and the only consolation we have received is a suggestion that individuals should build their own shelters, the do-it-yourself plan.
While speaking in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne last Monday the Prime Minister effectively answered a question I put to him earlier in the day and announced the formation of a royal commission, along the lines of the Hoover commission in the United States, to investigate the operations of the civil service of Canada. I view this with some misgivings because we who live in Ottawa have recollections of another similar investigation conducted by the union government after the first world war which spread fear and distrust among the civil service of the time and did nothing to enhance the prestige of the government or the operations of the civil service. Then, in the early part of the thirties, we had another investigation which only resulted in cutting wages and the firing of hundreds of civil servants. I can only hope that the personnel of the commission will be chosen from outstanding and able Canadians, that the inquiry will not necessarily follow the pattern in the United States and that the investigation in the several departments will not be of a type that may be likened to an inquisition. Above all, civil servants should be assured that their jobs are not at stake.
The determination of civil service salaries is, under law, a joint responsibility of the civil service commission and the government of the day. Section 11 of the Civil Service Act states:
The commission shall, from time to time, as may be necessary, recommend rates of compensation


for any new classes that may be established hereunder. and may propose changes in the rates of compensation for existing classes.
Although the commission proposes, it is the cabinet and parliament which dispose because the section goes on to say:
Proposed rates of compensation shall become operative only upon their approval by the governor in council, and, where any increased expenditure will result therefrom, when parliament has provided the money required for such increased expenditure.
Throughout the years, Mr. Speaker, the never ending process of civil service salary determination has resulted in the development and acceptance of certain principles which should guide those involved in the process, including the government itself. Succeeding governments have enunciated these principles. The Prime Minister said in May, 1958:
For many years it has been generally accepted that two main principles should guide the determination of salaries in the service. First, the salaries must be enough to do the job, that is, to attract enough of the right kind of men and women into the service and keep them in it. Second, they must be fair as between civil servants and people outside the service, the taxpayers if you will, which means that the salaries we pay for any class of work should be comparable with those paid by private employers for similar classes of work, taking into account the other terms of employment that are necessary to make a fair comparison. I think these principles should continue to guide us.
He also said on this occasion:
We are fortunate in having in the commission persons of outstanding ability and longstanding records of outstanding work as career civil servants with a wide variety of experience.
Fulfilling its responsibility under the Civil Service Act, in June, 1959 the commission recommended an increase for most classes of civil servants, averaging about 8 per cent. The recommendation for increase was based on a comparison of civil service salaries with those prevailing outside for similar classes of employment as of October 1, 1958. The recommendations included a suggestion that the increases be made effective and retroactive to the date on which the comparisons were made. It did not include, of course, or take into account any gains which will have been made by private employers since October 1, 1958.
Then, on July 9, 1959, in answer to a question the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) informed the House of Commons that he had received the recommendations of the civil service commission, but that the matter was still under discussion between the civil service commission and the minister. Then, on October 13, the Minister of Finance, without prior warning, told the joint action committee that the government would not implement the commission's recommendations. He

stated in the press release issued on the same day that, even apart from financial considerations, the government was not prepared to accept the commission's recommendations. Following a prior announcement by the Prime Minister in May, 1958, which I have quoted,
I believe that the civil servants of Canada had a right to expect last year that the recommendations of the pay research bureau, which was established by the present government, and the civil service commission, should have been granted and made retroactive to October, 1958.
The figures contained in the report of the dominion bureau of statistics on industry salaries, as of October, 1958, show the average weekly salary to be $93.74 as compared to $72 for civil servants. Comparable studies of individual salary classes have already been placed on Hansard by the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron), and I shall not repeat them at this time. The government owes it to its employees, to take the necessary steps to grant the recommended increases immediately.
I should repeat that since October 9, 1958 wages in industry have increased. Even if the increases were granted, civil servants' salaries would still lag behind industry.
The government in reaching its decision seems to have decided to accept the political risks involved in the interests of a better balanced budget, yet it seems doubtful that it is really in the public interest to hew to a policy which identifies the government as a cheap employer and scares away from government service those persons who feel that their skills are of a high standard and worth the going rates. The enunciated principles of pay determination in the public service are the only principles by which Canada can maintain a high calibre civil service. Civil servants do not want to strike, nor should they strike, but I believe that the government will have to consider immediately granting to civil servants bargaining rights such as exist in industry. Surely, employees of the crown are entitled to settle their grievances in the same manner as municipal employees, and to talk across the table to their employer without fear or favour when it comes to a matter of wages or conditions of work. I should like also to remind some members of this house that all civil servants are not in Ottawa, but that less than a third of the total number live in this area. Most government employees live in other parts of the country. In my opinion, it would be well for many other members of this house to reassess their thinking.
I should like to say a word on behalf of pensioned civil servants, widows and dependents of deceased civil servants. A year ago the Minister of Finance announced a plan giving a supplementary payment to a
The Address-Mr. J. T. Richard certain group of pensioners. This was a step in the right direction, but hardly enough because the cost of living has gone up since that time. I should hope that the minister would find a way to increase these pensions by at least half the amount already granted. The cost of the plan has been very low. It is not a permanent charge since it applies only to a limited number of civil servants who retired before a certain date.
May I be allowed now, Mr. Speaker, to say just a few words about trading stamps.
I agree with what was said by the hon. member for York-Humber (Miss Aitken) during this debate. She said that we in this parliament believe in free enterprise and in the minimum of government interference with the rights of individuals to buy and sell in the open market. I agree with her also when she said that the women of this country are not easily fooled; that they are as intelligent as the merchant who is selling to them and as intelligent as the women of other countries. They are as shrewd and as astute buyers as you will find anywhere. I think that is a well deserved tribute to the women of our country, and I was glad to hear the hon. member for York-Humber say these things during her speech a few days ago.
I should like to say a few words now about the national capital plan. I hope that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) will find time to give this matter his immediate attention. He should find excellent sites on Sussex street for the erection of some fine buildings. There is a very sore spot now right next to the Connaught building where the income tax department is lodged in a wooden shelter. This should be torn down as soon as possible and replaced with an edifice in keeping with the area. I ask the Minister of Public Works also to state formally that the government is ready and willing, at any time, to put up a very substantial share of the cost of erecting a bridge between Ottawa and Hull. I quite agree that we have had no assurance from either of the provincial governments to date that they are willing to share in the expense of erecting such a bridge. However, may I repeat that in my opinion the whole cost of the bridge, excluding the approaches, could well be borne by the federal government.
I should like also to ask the Minister of Public Works to instruct the national capital commission and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, in co-operation with the city of Ottawa, to plan the development of the lower town area around Sussex street in such a way that the residents will not be displaced. As Minister of Public Works I trust also that in the distribution of moneys to be made available for housing loans he will draft

The Address-Mr. J. T. Richard regulations which will encourage the money to be used for the construction of homes within the reach of those who need them most. There are too many of the loans just now directed to the construction of houses which cost $16,000 or more. The man who really needs a house today is looking for a home which he can buy at a price ranging between $7,500 and $12,000, with a minimum deposit of about $500. He cannot find such a house at the present time.
In the speech from the throne, it was announced that certain revisions would be made to the Expropriation Act. For 12 years I have been the lone voice in this house speaking once a year about the antiquity and inequity of the Expropriation Act in its application. I hope that the amendments which the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) will introduce will not make it easier for the government to expropriate at a cheaper price. There are certain expropriations which, of course, are necessary. However, it must be realized eventually that expropriation in itself is not only a hardship to the owner but an impingement on his civil right to property. Expropriation should be exercised with great fairness, even favouring the party expropriated. I am thinking particularly of those expropriations that have to be made for the national capital plan. I trust that we will have an opportunity of looking at the contents of the bill at an early date before it is discussed, and that it will reveal that a thorough assessment has been made of the rights of citizens who are involved in expropriation proceedings.
I cannot close without another plea for a Canadian flag, Mr. Speaker. Our 100th birthday is an excellent time to step forward with a distinctively Canadian flag, one which has meaning for all our citizens and under which we can all unite. It could be a symbolic fulfilment of nationhood. During the session of 1950, on April 17, I had the privilege of introducing a resolution to that effect. Strange as it may seem to some of the new members, in the presence of the three leaders of the parties in the house at the time, the Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent, the Hon. George Drew, and Mr. Coldwell, the motion was agreed to unanimously, but nothing came of it. Other similar motions since that date have been talked out. I am sure that if a referendum were held at this time throughout the country the great majority of our people would favour a truly distinctive Canadian flag. At the same time, we should formally recognize "O Canada" as our national anthem. It is now sung everywhere in this country, and when it is played at large gatherings and meetings all Canadians stand up with pride. Let us, Mr. Speaker, pledge ourselves to give 
Canada a flag and national anthem on the one hundredth anniversary of confederation.

speakeroldname: Mr. E. L. Morris (Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne I would wish that I might be possessed, if only for a few moments, of that characteristic felicity of phrase which has been so evident throughout your term, sir; and also, if I may say so, in the speech of the mover of the address in reply, the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Morissette), and in the speech of the seconder, the hon. and gracious member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman).
It is my wish, Mr. Speaker, to speak for a few moments about a matter affecting the whole House of Commons having to do with provincial representation in this House of Commons. The British North America Act of 1867 provided that in respect of representation in this house the province of Quebec should enjoy 65 members, and that the other provinces would be entitled to a number of members representing the quotient resulting from dividing the population of Quebec by 65, and then taking each of the separate provincial populations and dividing it by the quotient so resulting.
The act also provided that on the completion of the decennial census of 1871, and at each subsequent decennial census-the next is to occur in 1961-the representation of the several provinces should be readjusted from time to time provided that the proportionate representation of the provinces as prescribed in the act was maintained. This formula, namely the province of Quebec having the fixed number of 65 members, and to each other province a number being assigned as its population compared with the division of the quotient of 65 into Quebec's population, prevailed in 20 general elections, until and after the 1945 federal general election.
In the session of parliament in 1946 the House of Commons adopted a resolution which stated that the effect of the provisions of the British North America Act relating to representation had not been entirely satisfactory in that proportionate representation of the provinces according to population had not been maintained, and that a more equitable apportionment of members to the various provinces would be effected if readjustments were made on the basis of the population of the provinces taken as a whole. Accordingly, the British North America Act was amended in 1946 to provide a new rule to regulate the representation in the House of Commons. Representation was therein fixed as follows.
The membership assigned to each province shall be computed by dividing the total population of

the provinces by two hundred and fifty-four and by dividing the population of each province by the quotient so obtained.
This rule, Mr. Speaker, employed in the redistribution of representation made in 1947, was effective in the general election of 1949.
From 1867 to 1945, and inclusive of the general election in 1945, the province of Quebec had 65 members in the House of Commons. Ontario's membership varied as its population varied, from 82 rising to 92; but at the end of the term in 1945 it was perhaps coincidental that Ontario's representation in the House of Commons was identical, 82, with its representation at the time of confederation, and that Quebec's was identical with 65.
The effect of the revision of 1946 which provided the rule that the membership should be computed by dividing the total population of all provinces by 254, and then dividing the population of each province by the quotient so resulting, was to increase Ontario's representation by only one seat, to 83, Quebec's representation from 65 to 73, Nova Scotia's from 12 to 13, and British Columbia's from 16 to 18. Alberta remained unchanged at its then figure of 17; Saskatchewan declined from 21 to 20, and Manitoba declined from 17 to 16.
After the completion of the last decennial census in 1951 it became apparent to the then members of parliament that, as a result mostly of a wartime shift in population, a substantial reduction in the representation of the province of Saskatchewan would take place if the 1946 rule continued to be imposed. Accordingly, in an effort to eliminate sharp reductions from one decennial census to another, the British North America Act was again amended to provide representation on a changed basis. Rule 1 of subsection 1 of section 51 was amended to read:
-there shall be assigned to each of the provinces a number of members computed by dividing the total population of the provinces by two hundred and sixty-one and by dividing the population of each province by the quotient so obtained-
Rule 3 said:
Notwithstanding anything in this section, if upon completion of a computation under rules one and two, the number of members to be assigned to a province is less than the number of senators representing the said province, rules one and two shall cease to apply in respect of the said province, and there shall be assigned to the said province a number of members equal to the said number of senators.
Rule 5 said:
On any such readjustment the number of members for any province shall not be reduced by more than 15 per cent below the representation to which such province was entitled under rules one to four of this subsection at the last preceding readjustment of the representation of that province, and there shall be no reduction in the rep-
The Address-Mr. Morris resentation of any province as a result of which that province would have a smaller number of members than any other province that, according to the results of the then last decennial census, did not have a larger population.
Mr. Speaker, the principal effect of these new rules is that representation of any province shall not be reduced by more than 15 per cent at any one readjustment subject, however, to the qualification that the rule shall not operate in such manner that the representation of a province with a smaller population shall be greater than any province with a larger population.
Subsequently parliament enacted a new measure. "An act to readjust the representation in the House of Commons, 1952." Section 2 provided:
Eighty-five members of the House of Commons shall be elected for the province of Ontario, seventy-five for the province of Quebec, twelve for the province of Nova Scotia, ten for the province of New Brunswick, fourteen for the province of Manitoba, twenty-two for the province of British Columbia, four for the province of Prince Edward Island, seventeen for the province of Saskatchewan, seventeen for the province of Alberta, seven for the province of Newfoundland, one for the Yukon territory, and one for Mackenzie district of the Northwest Territories, thus making a total of 265 members.
It is this basis which was utilized in the elections of 1957 and 1958.
The application of the rule of proportional representation since confederation has produced a strange result in the Atlantic provinces. Frequently in the past, and in this parliament, members from the Atlantic provinces, happily for us, joined frequently now by hon. members from other provinces, have spoken eloquently and persistently about some of the so-called disabilities of the Atlantic provinces. Generally speaking, all political parties have acknowledged to some degree or other that the Atlantic province area inherited from the British North America Act a sequence of disabilities. We are not agreed as to the nature of these disabilities, nor are we agreed as to the extent of them, but all political parties in Canadian history have at one time or another acknowledged the presence of some adverse effect of confederation upon the Atlantic provinces.
In the working out of the basis of representation in the House of Commons, we in the Atlantic provinces feel that not only are we asked to support whatever degree of disability has come to us through confederation but that we have also, in fact, been asked to bear it with fewer and fewer members.
It is now said it is likely that the decennial census of 1961 will produce a further diminution in the representation of my province- Nova Scotia-and that we will return 11
57S	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Morris members instead of 12. Already the provinces of Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick are required to have recourse to the arbitrary standard of the number of senators as a means of determining the number of members in the House of Commons. Prince Edward Island would not be entitled to four members in this house if any other rule were applied. My own constituency of Halifax has a population nearly two and a half times that of the entire province of Prince Edward Island, but Prince Edward Island, thankfully, can have recourse to the rule which says that its representation shall not be diminished below the number of senators, and because it has four senators-two of these seats acquired at the time of its entrance into confederation from Nova Scotian senatorial representation, and two from New Brunswick, because this was the formula arrived at in 1867 when Prince Edward Island entered confederation, that these four senators would be drawn two from one province and two from another-it must have a minimum of four members.
I say it brings no great credit to successive governments since confederation that the only areas in this whole country which have suffered a diminution in membership have all been in the Atlantic provinces so-called. In 1867 when Nova Scotia joined confederation we had 19 members. In 1872, 1874, 1878, 1882, 1887 and 1891 we had 21 members. We have gone steadily down since then. We are down now to 12 and they say we shall go down to 11. However, we cannot go below 10 unless you change the rule of a floor as to numbers dependent on the number of senators. New Brunswick had 15 members at the time of confederation, which number rose to 16 and is now down to 10. Prince Edward Island had six members starting in the general election of 1874. The number never rose above six and the province has had four seats since 1904, a number which was supported during part of that time by the number of its senatorial seats. Newfoundland has seven members and its representation could be reduced by one; it would amount to six based on the number of its senators.
Our population is growing too fast.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
speechtext:
The Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Browne) interjects that the population is growing too fast. We are delighted to hear that the Newfoundland membership will be seven. We would be delighted if it went up to 20, or 30 or 50. The point I am making is that the historic Atlantic provinces area shows a tendency which flies in the face of his observation. The policies deriving from confederation-the things we


have done as a nation-have produced a diminution in our population relative to the rest of the country, so our representation has declined. In 1867 Nova Scotia and New Brunswick together had 34 members; now they have 22. The burden of my case is simply this; to some degree or other, we in the Atlantic area have suffered the disabilities of confederation, and subtly and stealthily the things we could do to contend with these disabilities have been restricted because our representation in the house itself is being gradually taken away from us.
Our request from the Atlantic area is: do not talk to us about diminishing our numbers. Give us back the members with which we entered confederation. Oh, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) may smile. It is amusing for him, perhaps, to know that the diminution of which I have been speaking took place under Liberal government. But it is not amusing to us, to those who have to contend with it.
In the Atlantic provinces area we have many forces with which to contend. I do not suggest that a change in the Representation Act, chapter 334 of the acts of 1952, is going to be made as a result of this one speech, but I do say that this should be done. In the last session, the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), about whom I shall have something to say in a moment, drew to the attention of this house that we were going to suffer the loss of yet another member. I wish to say simply this; we do not wish to suffer the loss of another member. We would like to have back the seven members we have lost. If the province of Saskatchewan, or any other province, enjoys a sufficient representation, then we agree with this. But we do not think that the drop in representation should be so precipitate as to reduce it by more than 15 per cent in one decennial period. What, in the long run, is the difference between a slow wearing away and an accelerated wearing away in a 10-year period?
Mr. Speaker, may I have the unanimous consent of the house to place on Hansard for the convenience of hon. members a table showing the representation in the House of Commons as at federal general elections from 1867 to 1958. I might say that this is an exact copy of the table which appeared in the Canada Year Book, page 50, with the single addition that I have entered the year 1958, since the representation was identical with 1953 and 1957.

speechtext: Has the hon. member leave to have the table referred to by him incorporated into the Hansard record?
Agreed.

speechtext:
The Address-Mr. Morris
Mr. Speaker, may I thank hon. members in all parts of the house for agreeing to having the table included.
I should not have made any plea for any change in representation in this house unless I had considered what it might be that members of parliament might be doing here. Certainly if we had 12 members from Nova Scotia who did not perform any useful purpose for Nova Scotia there would be little point in asking that they be returned to their original number. I therefore recently reflected on the functions of a member of parliament as we on this side of the house conceive those functions to be. In doing so I have been interested in observing the itinerant views expressed on this matter by the hon. member for Port Arthur who I note has recently been described in the press as the poor man's Socrates.
I should like to discuss for a few moments the impressions expressed by the hon. member for Port Arthur relating to members of parliament. We were all at home in our constituencies doing those grubby little things which I know the hon. member finds unequal to membership in this house when we read that we in the House of Commons are all phonies. This was a remark attributed to the hon. member in an address at Victoria College. But our verbose friend did not confine himself to describing members of the house as phonies. He went a little further and said that we had a phony British North America Act. He said, further that we had a phony constitution. He then went on to say there were some phony aspects to the royal tour. The royal party will be overjoyed at hearing that. He said that members of parliament who went out to their constituencies and had pictures taken with the royal couple were engaging in a phony activity. He said that he stayed away. I for one did not stay away. I thought the royal couple performed a valuable service in visiting my constituency and I doubt if many hon. members feel differently. I did not, however, have my photograph taken with the royal pair.
The hon. member concluded his remarks by saying that a university education enables one to spot people who are phony. I thought to myself how thankful I must be that I have had a university education because now I can spot phonies. Apparently we all stand indicted. In the view of this hon. gentleman we are all phonies with a phony constitution, hosts to phony royal visits and having a phony stance. But we are not quite finished with this dialogue of penance. Apparently members of parliament are something more than phonies.
Last Thursday the hon. gentleman divested himself of a few more views. He said that

last session he had raised in the house a grievance-as we all recalled-and	had
spoken for higher salaries for members of parliament. I remember the hon. gentleman's speech very well. I recall how surprised I was at learning that the century of the common man was to be ushered in by professing socialists who were decrying the fact that an annual salary of $10,000 was not sufficient. This is not unlike Stanley Knowles launching the new party of the common man by organizing a dinner in the Chateau Laurier at $50 a plate. This is going to be some century, and I want to be around to witness the era of the common man in which his spokesman in this house cannot get by on a salary of $10,000 a year.
But the hon. gentleman said also that he had some second thoughts, that he now recognizes that there are some nuances in connection with the inferior salary. There probably are some nuances in connection with the salary of members of parliament. One of the nuances he mentioned was that in his opinion most Canadians thought members of parliament were overpaid. That would be a nuance if it were true. I might say that if the Canadian people do not think so it is not, in my opinion, in any way attributable to the fact that the hon. gentleman has refrained from trying to inculcate this suspicion among them. His going around the country describing members as phonies would scarcely encourage people to give us a bigger salary. But there is more to it than this. We cannot be confined just to phonies.
Last Thursday the hon. gentleman informed us that he finds our present parliamentary procedure decadent, so we all stand indicted as a generation of vipers. We are phonies, people caught up in a decadent system. And finally-this is perhaps the harshest touch of all-the hon. member told a member of the parliamentary press gallery during the last recess that an examination of the records of the library of parliament would reveal that this is one of the most illiterate parliaments Canada ever had. So you go down to the parliamentary library and you count up the number of entries in the charge book against your name and if you have not a certain number of entries you are illiterate. According to this hon. gentleman, who says he has a university education and is now in a position to spot phonies, we are now to measure literacy in this country among members of parliament solely on the basis of the number of books that have been charged to our names on the record of the library of parliament.
I cannot resist commenting that I come from a part of the country that was well established at a time when Port Arthur was

just a small, pleasant, leafy Ontario town and there we do not measure literacy on the basis of how many books you take out of the library. We do not even measure university education on that basis nor do we conceive the purpose of a university education to be to equip one to recognize phonies. I thought at the time I heard about the hon. gentleman's philosophy how nice it must be to be a total ideologist, a man who has a doctrinaire answer for everyone, a criteria for literacy.
I urge my fellow hon. members of this house who do not want to be tagged as phonies, illiterates or as decadent by the hon. member for Port Arthur to rush into the parliamentary library. To them I say, do not order any particular books, get them by the pound. Make sure that at the end of the session when you go home you have more books charged out to your discredit than you have ever had before. Go back among your people and say, "I have been talking to a university graduate and this how you measure literacy."
The hon. member during the recess must have encountered a number of nuances because he announced that he was not going to come back here. I notice he did not answer the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) when that question was put to him the other day. The hon. member did not take that opportunity to confirm his intention. However, during the recess he did announce that he was not coming back, that he would not run again. "Atlas Shrugged". He had been to Ottawa, he said, and if I may paraphrase:
In the house, the M.P. is expected only to stay awake and be ready to pound his desk when his leader makes a speech. Most of his energy and practically all his thought is to be devoted to attending the fall fairs in his riding, mouthing greetings to local Kiwanis clubs-
How the Kiwanians will love that. I continue:
-and shaking hands with home town voters.
So, if you do anything other than contemplate the great problems of the world when you are elected as a member of parliament you are not doing your job at all but are just politicking. No sense of duty is allowed to creep into the hon. member's suspicion. There is no sense of realization that there are other hon. members of this house with small children and families whom they dearly miss but who remain here and do their job out of a sense of duty.
Duty is a sweet word which has apparently gone out of the social vocabulary. He wants us to be turned into a nation of government workers. He announced between sessions of parliament that he did not think this imposed socialism on the Canadian 79951-0-37J
The Address-Mr. Morris Labour Congress was a good idea. He had some quotations to that effect. He repeated them the other day. He spoke in the house in this debate of other people who have an idea of the party, and then he went on to say, as reported at page 439 of Hansard:
I do not argue that this has gone down to the grass roots yet.
What we are witnessing here is the laying on of a political party. Somebody gets the idea when he is defeated for the House of Commons, and so he goes out and says to the labour movement, "Here, I am going to lay upon you a political organization, not from the grass roots up but from the top down," and then they come into the House of Commons. I must say, because I stand indicted, I am decadent, I am obviously illiterate; I do not take as many books out of the library as the hon. gentleman. I come here and I sit down; I come from a province where representative government started in this country, where responsible government started in this country, and I am to be told that I do not know what parliamentary democracy is. What it is, I am told, is the laying on of a political party upon unsuspecting, unwilling millions of workers.
I say to the hon. gentleman this: you want us to be turned into a nation of government workers, evangelizing every corner of this land with the latest information on subjects such as hog raising, pedagogy, vegetable canning, road making and carpet laying. You want us to become a nation of civil servants waging eternal war upon hookworm, patent medicines, white slavery, foot-and-mouth disease, cholera infantum, adultery and rum.
You want us to have civil servants running around chastising Canadians for having these things and I say we want no part of it; we want no part of an imposed party organization. Too many phonies in parliament, too many phonies outside parliament, think that parliamentary democracy is held in the close embrace of a few wizards who have spent a few years in parliament and who profess knowledge of parliament and its ways and then go out and lay upon people an imposed political organization. Those people managed to wreck the only evidence of a C.C.F. party we had, and they will probably wreck the labour movement as well. You want to impose a socialist party; we had an imposed party of another kind. Then, I say, if I disagree with this, surely the test of illiteracy is yet to be seen.
Mr. Speaker, who am I? A crude Tory backbencher stands revealed in all his shame as a phony, a phony who happens to love parliament, who has a fondness for the constitution, who has an affection for the royal

The Address-Mr. Pickersgill family, who has a university education bought for him by the sacrifice of his parents. Who am I to say what is a phony? I stand indicted. I am a member of a decadent assembly; I must bow to the superior intelligence of those dreamy socialists who know all things. I am obviously illiterate because when I love a book I read it, as my finances allow I buy it; I cherish it and I do not make entries in the parliamentary library record in order to impress myself upon itinerant socialists. But, Mr. Speaker, now that I stand revealed as all other members on all sides of the house are for what we are, phonies, decadent and illiterate, may I say that speaking for my province, I understood that the people of Upper Musquodoboit sent me here to look after their troubles, because if I do not look after them and if I do not get a mail service at Sheet Harbour I can tell you for sure that the hon. member for Port Arthur will not get them for me because he says he cannot even grub for his own constituency. He has got to be working on the world level.
When we retire at night in the backwoods of Nova Scotia unversed, unsung, unrepresented and unheralded, we sometimes keep by our bed two volumes, one of which is the bible, well-thumbed from Tobias to Mark and Matthew.
According to the standards of literacy recently endowed upon this House of Commons, if you take the bible out of the parliamentary library you must get some other books as well. It is not sufficient to guide your life any more by the bible. Socialist standards of literacy require you to read it with a reasonable degree of unconcern and judge its lessons against other books. But we in Nova Scotia, being illiterate as we are, get our sustenance out of the bible; we get a little technical comfort from the sayings of Sam Slick of Slickville, the itinerant watchmaker who, you might say, espoused a Conservative trade in a Liberal way. My idea of a degree of literacy is founded on one remark of Sam Slick. I know it will be new to the nation but I rise to do the very best I can to reveal the best I can. It is this. I might say I give it verbatim and unexpurgated. Sam Slick said one day: "Whenever you make an impression on a newspaper man, stop. Your reasonin' and the details may ruin you."

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS AS AT FEDERAL GENERAL ELECTIONS 1867-1958
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope the senior hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Morris) will not expect me to follow him in his grubbing in Upper Musquodoboit, but I am quite ready to match him wharf for wharf any time he wants to.


I have risen today, to support the amendment moved by my leader. I do not intend to read it all because it is repeated every day in the Votes and Proceedings, but I want to draw attention particularly to one part of the amendment, and I am leaving out the words that I do not intend particularly to deal with:
This house is of the opinion that the failure of the government to provide full and accurate information, is a major cause of the confusion and uncertainty that prevails-
I am going to have something to say about this failure to provide full and accurate information about the public affairs of this country that has characterized the government of this country since June 21, 1957, and which is growing worse with every television appearance of the leader of the government. But before I say anything about the appearances of the leader of the government, that is to say, the nominal leader of the government, I wish first to say that I intend to deal with the real speech from the throne.
The real speech from the throne for this session was not delivered by His Excellency in the other place, and it was not written by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker). I hope it will be no disrespect to His Excellency if I speak of the real speech from the throne which, with his usual modesty, was written by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) seeing himself as prime minister and to make doubly sure, with his usual modesty, delivered by the Minister of Finance apparently envisaging himself as Governor General, before the Canadian Club of Toronto. With his usual modesty the Minister of Finance described that speech as a report on the state of the nation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS AS AT FEDERAL GENERAL ELECTIONS 1867-1958
speechtext: No, he did not.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS AS AT FEDERAL GENERAL ELECTIONS 1867-1958
speechtext:
Would the hon. gentleman like me to apprise him of his words? I have the text that he issued right here and he will find that he said in that speech that it was the last opportunity he would have before the session of parliament opened to report on the state of the nation.
I do not intend to follow the Minister of Finance through all the 22 pages of this speech because I prefer to make my own. But I do intend to give to hon. members my own interpretation and I think it will be found to be a very accurate summary of the speech that was made to the Canadian Club on January 12 by the Minister of Finance reporting on the state of the nation, apparently envisaging himself as the head of the government. This will be my interpretation of what the minister said there. I do not want anyone

to say I am quoting the hon. gentleman because I am not doing that. But what he said in effect was that this country had gone through the longest and most expensive financial spree in its history; that he, the Minister of Finance was now having the worst hangover a minister of finance had ever had, and the worst part of that hangover was that he had discovered that Walter Harris had been right all the time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS AS AT FEDERAL GENERAL ELECTIONS 1867-1958
speechtext: This is certainly your interpretation. It is about as far from fact as day is from night.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS AS AT FEDERAL GENERAL ELECTIONS 1867-1958
speechtext:
It is my interpretation which has been shared by practically the whole press of this country, as I will show the hon. gentleman before I finish. But there was one phrase in that speech that simply doubled me up. Nobody but the Minister of Finance, with that bubbling sense of fun of his, could possibly have uttered this phrase, but here it is. "Consistency", said the Minister of Finance, "what a gem thou art." After swallowing everything he said in 1956 and 1957 and saying most of the things Mr. Harris was saying at that time he said, "Consistency, what a gem thou art."
The minister of course has a Churchillian touch-I mean the great Churchill of course- that is not given to most of us in this house, and he ended his speech like the great Churchill standing on the beaches. I cannot forbear giving the house the minister's climax:
The message which I should like to convey to Canadians at the threshold of this new year and decade therefore is a challenge in simple terms: Work and save.
Work and save. Three quarters of a million Canadians are saying to the government today, give us work and we will do the saving. "Consistency, what a gem thou art."

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS AS AT FEDERAL GENERAL ELECTIONS 1867-1958
speechtext: What does Joey say?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS AS AT FEDERAL GENERAL ELECTIONS 1867-1958
speechtext:
"Work and save", says the Minister of Finance, but what does the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill), that lesser Churchill, say? He says, "Dry your tears, never mind saving; borrow from the United States, it will come out all right in the end." Consistency, what a gem thou art.
Going back again to the Canadian Club in Toronto and the real speech from the throne, I would say that anyone who reads this speech carefully will find that this speech, in so far as enlightening the public is concerned, was like trying to play Hamlet without the prince of Denmark. All the causes of our present tight money situation are given
The Address-Mr. Pickersgill except the real cause and that is completely left out. Does the minister say anywhere in that speech from beginning to end that during the period of economic advancement in 1956 the government of that day was paying off the debt? Does he tell us that in the year 1956-57, the last full year the Liberal government was in office, the net national debt of this country was reduced by $1 billion? What, in other words, did Mr. Harris do when there was a demand for credit from the banks? He paid off the national debt to the extent of $1 billion so that would be available for other Canadians to use.
But what is this minister doing in a similar position? I admit that he managed to pay off a very small amount of the debt up until March 31, 1958, out of Mr. Harris' savings, but when he had exhausted them he started in on this spree and since that time the debt of the country has been increased by $2 billion and is still being increased. That, is the real cause of the tight money policy. It is the real cause of high interest rates. It is that $2 billion borrowed in less than two years that has bid up interest rates. When the Prime Minister talks about the biggest borrower in the country, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance are the biggest borrowers in the country, overwhelmingly the biggest borrowers in the country, and they are directly responsible for the interest rates that everyone else has to pay, if indeed they are allowed to pay them at all.
I told the minister that I would repeat to him in slightly different language what he said in his speech. I said that he had said that Walter Harris had been right all the time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS AS AT FEDERAL GENERAL ELECTIONS 1867-1958
speechtext: I say you are crazy to say a thing like that.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS AS AT FEDERAL GENERAL ELECTIONS 1867-1958
speechtext: I beg your pardon?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS AS AT FEDERAL GENERAL ELECTIONS 1867-1958
speechtext:
I say you are
crazy to say a thing like that. There is no resemblance to fact. Can you not stick to the fact once in a while?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS AS AT FEDERAL GENERAL ELECTIONS 1867-1958
speechtext:
When the minister has concluded all these extraordinarily erudite interruptions such as "crazy" and "nonsense" that are so dear to his heart, perhaps I might be allowed to continue. This is what the Victoria Times had to say about the minister's speech in Toronto, about the real speech from the throne, and lest you have any compunction about this, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I heartily endorse every word of it and make it my own, though I

The Address-Mr. Pickersgill hasten to add that I did not write it. The editorial is headed, "Mr. Fleming's Confession", and reads:
Mr. Fleming's remarkable speech in Toronto this week repudiates the original policies of the government and isolates its paramount problem in the session of parliament opening tomorrow. While the government secured election on a policy of easy credit, Mr. Fleming now demands credit restriction.
While Mr. Diefenbaker, only a few weeks ago. was attacking the private banks for lending too little money, Mr. Fleming now urges them to restrict their loans. While the former Liberal government was condemned, year in and year out, for forcing up interest rates, Mr. Fleming now blandly announces that these rates are likely to remain high for an indefinite period.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS AS AT FEDERAL GENERAL ELECTIONS 1867-1958
speechtext: I did not.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS AS AT FEDERAL GENERAL ELECTIONS 1867-1958
speechtext:
I continue:
While Mr. Diefenbaker's famous vision involved capital expansion in all directions at breakneck speed, Mr. Fleming now asks Canada to moderate its investment lest it produce another round of inflation, followed by another business recession.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS AS AT FEDERAL GENERAL ELECTIONS 1867-1958
speechtext: I did not do anything of the kind.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS AS AT FEDERAL GENERAL ELECTIONS 1867-1958
speechtext:
I continue:
And while the government, having promised to cut total spending, plunged immediately into record budgets and record deficits, Mr. Fleming now warns everybody to go easy because the nation cannot afford to maintain its recent pace.
That is characteristic of the kind of thing that has been said about the real speech from the throne, the report on the state of the nation of the Minister of Finance temporarily envisaging himself in the role of head of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS AS AT FEDERAL GENERAL ELECTIONS 1867-1958
speechtext:
It is not a bit
characteristic of the press statements, the true press.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS AS AT FEDERAL GENERAL ELECTIONS 1867-1958
speechtext:
As a matter of fact, although I cannot do it with clarity I can just imagine the Minister of Finance in the role of prime minister. I can just imagine it. I say I could not imagine it with the clarity with which he does and I feel sure that if he ever attained it he would be a very bad one.
But we had also the spectacle a few months ago of the Prime Minister apparently thinking he was the minister of finance and that, sir, strained my credulity as I am sure it will strain the credulity of the house and the country quite beyond the breaking point.
When I came back from Newfoundland at the beginning of September-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS AS AT FEDERAL GENERAL ELECTIONS 1867-1958
speechtext: You were there, were you?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS AS AT FEDERAL GENERAL ELECTIONS 1867-1958
speechtext: Oh, yes, I was in Newfoundland. I went there just as soon as the hon. member's prolonging of the session enabled me to get there.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS AS AT FEDERAL GENERAL ELECTIONS 1867-1958
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS AS AT FEDERAL GENERAL ELECTIONS 1867-1958
speechtext: You promised to build a house there, too.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS AS AT FEDERAL GENERAL ELECTIONS 1867-1958
speechtext:
If it would comfort the hon. member for Saint John-Albert, I may say that while I was there I built myself a house, and it is a very nice house. If he would like to come and stay with me I would be glad to have him for a day or two.
Let us get back to the temporary Minister of Finance. The Prime Minister, speaking at Kitimat as reported in the Ottawa Citizen of August 25, said, and this is in quotation marks:
-Today the chartered banks had the greatest reserves in their history, a figure in the neighbourhood ol $7 billion.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS AS AT FEDERAL GENERAL ELECTIONS 1867-1958
speechtext: That statement was not made, and it was immediately denied.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS AS AT FEDERAL GENERAL ELECTIONS 1867-1958
speechtext: As a matter of fact, when I read that the Prime Minister had mistaken the debts of the bank for their reserves, when I read that liabilities had become assets in the eyes of this government and that the more national debt we have the richer we are, it looked to me as though the Prime Minister was trying to take the public, like Alice, through the looking glass. You remember when that happened that Alice, like the public, found it dreadfully confusing, until the white queen, like the Prime Minister, explained, that's the effect of living backwards; it always makes one a little giddy at first."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS AS AT FEDERAL GENERAL ELECTIONS 1867-1958
speechtext: You should know.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS AS AT FEDERAL GENERAL ELECTIONS 1867-1958
speechtext:
The Prime Minister's budget speech came on T.V. I think we all recall the day, on October 1, after he had had a brief holiday, which so many of us begrudged him, that holiday in Quebec. I feel sure that the budget speech the Prime Minister delivered over T.V. on October 1 must have left the Minister of Finance very giddy as it did many others in this country. In that speech the Prime Minister told us, in the first place, that this was a report.
I am going to report to you on the state of the Canadian economy-
It is for this reason I call it a budget speech.
[DOT]-and those aspects which most closely affect the daily lives of the Canadian people.
What did we learn from the Prime Minister? We learned that this government had cured unemployment; that it had ended inflation. Then the Prime Minister began to talk about money and the speech really became interesting, informative and enlightening. Here is what the Prime Minister said:
But I have to be frank with you. Recovery has brought about a new set of difficulties.

I should think it has.
The most complex problems have come with the amazing speed and strength of the phenomenal economic recovery in Canada. A question has arisen over individual commercial bank credit. Some call it "the tight money situation".
Then, the Prime Minister, after saying that they were not like the Liberals, and they did not do anything about it except increase the debt of the country by $2 billion- he did not say that; I do not accuse the Prime Minister of telling us the facts. The Prime Minister said:
There is no such policy today.
No such policy of tight money.
What has happened is in consequence of natural economic forces, resulting from the demands of the phenomenal economic recovery. Interest rates have gone up.
Even the Prime Minister could not deny that, but that was no fault of this government. In March, 1958, when the interest rate had temporarily gone down, the Prime Minister told us, "We got it down for you". He went right across the country saying that. When interest rates come down the Prime Minister does it, but when they go up it is the economic forces of the country and not the $2 billion borrowing of the Minister of Finance. Oh, no, they have nothing to do with interest rates, nothing whatever.
The commercial banks have restricted their lending operations-
As a matter of fact, I do not know whether the figures really bear that out, but the Prime Minister said they had restricted their lending operations.
-with the result to the average man that money is harder and more costly to get-
Certainly, more costly.
-than has been the case heretofore.
Then, he went on to give us the remedy. Here is the remedy, what the government is going to do about it.
I want to make this clear, and abundantly clear: It is not the intention of the government to stand by and see small businessmen, and farmers, and home-builders, and small borrowers-
You know, all the little people about whom the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) loves to talk.
-denied their opportunity to share in the new prosperity of Canada by reason of arbitrary credit practices.
The Prime Minister was careful not to define what the arbitrary credit practices were, but he went on to tell us what he was going to do about it. Listen to it.
There is no simple solution to the situation.
It never seemed to occur to this government that if they had not gone into the money markets and borrowed $2 billion that would
The Address-Mr. Pickersgill otherwise have been available to other people the problem would not have existed in the form in which it is now existing.
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question. I do not want to spoil his speech.
No, I would be delighted.
Will he explain why it is that interest rates in the United States as well are much higher than they have been for 25 years? Is this govermnent responsible for that?
I shall be glad to explain that in any free time I am given after my 40-minute speech,-
Oh, oh.

-if the Prime Minister is really anxious for an explanation and this is not just another of those 15 per cent diversions which are so characteristic of the Prime Minister when he does not like what is being said. The Prime Minister said that there is no simple solution, and the fact the problem exists somewhere else is not going to solve it in Canada.
I've given thought to this;-
Just imagine the Prime Minister getting into his plane with books on economics and finance under his arm and he is going to study something about this economic business in all its aspects, and about the banks' reserves being higher than they have ever been before-

Mr. Speaker, I have
already said that I did not make that statement. I denied it the next day.

If the Prime Minister says he denied that statement the next day then I, of course, accept the denial at once. I made a very careful search of the newspapers before I made this speech and I noticed no denial of this statement. I would be very much obliged to the Prime Minister if he would show me the denial in print.
I've given thought to this; my colleagues and I have applied more days of study to this than to any matter before us.
Can you not see them, sir, hour after hour over there in the east block studying the interest rates and wondering if they could borrow another billion before the country went completely broke.
I have consulted with leaders in all walks of life. We are trying to arrive at a fair solution, but we are not going to take hasty action. I shall not be stampeded.
I assure you that there must be no runaway inflation in Canada. This danger, I believe, however can be avoided without denying the right of small businessmen and small borowers and farmers and the like-

The Address-Mr. Pickersgill
Whatever "the like" is.
-to share in Canada's growth.
My fellow Canadians, this is a time for confidence and faith. It's a time for the fullest consideration and the widest possible consultation. It's a time to explore all avenues to ensure a proper distribution of credit among the people who are entitled to share in it.
Perhaps one answer-
Perhaps it is not.
-is for the banks to reconsider their lending policies and rearrange their outstanding loans to the end that some large borrowers-
Like the Minister of Finance.
-will be taking less so that smaller borrowers can get more.
Whatever the final answer may be, it will only be determined after the fullest and most careful consultation and thought. I assure you this, that the government does not intend that the prosperity resulting from the economic recovery shall be for the benefit of the few, and to the frustration of the many.
Having put the banks in their place and solved the problem of the small borrowers, the Prime Minister went on to the next television show, instalment two of his budget speech. Instalment two of his budget speech was even more extraordinary than instalment one. This was his speech on what we old-fashioned Liberals, who were responsible for it, called social security, but what has been re-christened by the Prime Minister in order, no doubt, to give some people the impression that it is something new, and called social justice. What are we told by the Prime Minister?
I do not want to overburden you with statistics-
I may say he certainly did not, as I shall show in a moment-
-but there are times when the exact figures must be brought forward to give positive proof of the truth.
Direct payments to individuals by the dominion government on social justice account were $1,500 million last year, compared with $1 billion in the last year under the Liberals.
That statement is approximately correct. Perhaps I might even be unfair to the Prime Minister is saying that; it is correct. It may not be correct to the last dollar but it is correct in substance. But what the Prime Minister did not say, evidently for fear of overburdening us with too many statistics, was that of the $500 million increase since the fiscal year 1956-57, approximately $133 million was the direct result of those increases in all the social security payments recommended by Mr. Walter Harris in his budget in 1957. Nor did he say that $160 million of that figure was the cost for one year of the hospital insurance plan which my hon. friend for Essex East (Mr. Martin) piloted through this house and which was on the statute books before this government came into office. Nor did the Prime Minister say that $100 million


of this increase of $500 million was due to the increase in the population of Canada of those persons receiving those benefits, and with the immigration policy of this government, I doubt if the Prime Minister would take much credit for the increase in population.
Out of this whole amount of $500 million the Tory share is $106 million and the Liberal share, $293 million. Those were the statistics which we were not to be overburdened with. Those statistics were the estimates taken from the budget speeches and I think they will be found accurate as approximations; and that is all they are, as the Prime Minister's figure also was.
The other matter that the Prime Minister did not overburden the listeners with, was the fact that this government was responsible for increasing taxes to pay for this additional "social justice" to the tune of $352 million a year. That is the other side of the picture; but of course, that did not matter, it was not relevant. Let us see what the Prime Minister said about this. Let us see what he told the Canadian people. He said:
We have made-
I presume he means the government have made.
-in the last two and a half years, the greatest increases in Canadian history in the overall level of social justice benefits to every Canadian family in need of such assistance. We have done so in every category within the jurisdiction of the federal government and in many under the jurisdiction of the province, by joint action.
In two and a half years the Prime Minister claims the figure was $500 million, and of that $500 million, $293 million were due to the Liberals and $106 million to hon. members opposite. That is the kind of stuff the people are told. He was not content with that; he went on to say:
When we took office two and a half years ago we found the most astonishing evidence, far beyond what we had expected, of the shocking result of the careless inaction of the Liberal administration in its last years in office in this whole field of social justice.
What was that careless inaction? To increase the benefits by $293 million in the last year the Liberals were in office, and all the present government has done is to increase them by $106 million and send the Canadian people the bill for $352 million. Those are the real facts which were not included in the Prime Minister's budget speech of November 12.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are some of the bills you left unpaid, and you blame us for the deficit.

The Minister of Finance can make his speech afterwards and no doubt will.

Let us see what else we were told in the budget speech. I would not have time under the rules to deal with them all, although I would love to; but the other big thing this government did was in respect of payments to the provinces. The Prime Minister also told us about that. He did not overburden us with statistics on this question either. This is what he said:
In 1955-57, the last year the Liberals were in power, dominion government contributions to the provinces-
I might say that I would not have used the word "contributions", because there are many of these items that the provinces have a right to, and they are certainly not contributions from the federal government. The word I would use is "payments", but the Prime Minister said contributions. Continuing:
-not including payments to individuals, amounted to $689 million. For the present year the amount will be $1,212 million-an increase of 76 per cent. This extra assistance to the provinces has been of tremendous benefit not only to them but to the municipalities as well.
There is no doubt that that is true, no doubt whatever. The Prime Minister's figure is also true. But let us have a look at that figure. It represents an increase of $523 million. That is the same figure the Minister of Finance gave in the budget in one of the tables he prepared.
Does that not account, too, for the extra expenditure we made for the year?

That is another point, and I do not particularly appreciate the Prime Minister's diversion at this stage. Of this $523 million, $23 million was not a payment to the provinces at all, as I pointed out during the budget debate. It was a payment to municipalities and universities, and many of these universities are private institutions and are certainly not provinces. There was $500 million paid to the provinces, and of that $500 million the Minister of Finance-and I am using his figures-broke it down in this way: "Unconditional payments have increased by $195 million."
Let us have a look at these unconditional payments. Of the $195 million, $105 million was the result of the changes that Walter Harris recommended in 1956 to this house, which was voted when we were in office. The Tory share is $90 million. That is the unconditional grants.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But who found the money to pay them?

The taxpayers of Canada found the money.
The Address-Mr. Pickersgill

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And you blame us for having a deficit in meeting them.

The other part is the unconditional payments, and they have increased, according to the figures of the Minister of Finance, by $307 million. The Liberal's share of that is $210 million and the Tory share is $97 million. Those are the facts, and the Minister of Finance will find it quite impossible to controvert them, because they are from his own statistics which he produced in this house.
I have not said that the figures which the Prime Minister used were not correct. They were correct, but they were not complete. They were manipulated-a good parliamentary word these days-to give an untrue picture to the Canadian people. That is what happened, and how was it done? It was a very simple and plausible device, and it will no doubt be done again. They took the last full year we were in office, in which the payments provided for in 1956-57 which came into effect on April 1 of 1957 were not made, and they treated all the payments in 195758, practically all of which were the result of action taken by this parliament on the recommendation of the former Liberal government, as though they had been initiated by this government. I cannot think of any more thoroughly dishonest performance which has ever-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am sure the hon. member did not intend-at least, I hope he did not intend-to give the impression, or make the imputation, of dishonesty?

Oh no, sir. I am sorry the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai) is not in the house, because he heard me say this outside the house; I see he is here and I am now going to repeat it right here, and he will remember that I said it before. Oh no, sir, I do not think the Prime Minister did this at all. I do not think the Prime Minister knows what the figures are. I do not think the Prime Minister spends enough time in his office to find out what they are.
Mr. Speaker, so far I have enjoyed this speech with all its pantomime-
Order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the Prime Minister rising on a point of order?

Yes, I cannot allow even the hon. member to make a suggestion of dishonesty. It is a most unusual statement, and one that cannot be made having regard to the dignity of parliament.

The Address

Mr. Pickersgill
Withdraw.

I did not impute dishonesty to the Prime Minister or to any other member of this house. I was scrupulously careful to say that the figures the Prime Minister gave were correct. I am not now imputing dishonesty to the Prime Minister of any deliberate character, and if I have said anything which offends the Prime Minister's dignity I happily withdraw.
That is simply no withdrawal and I ask for a withdrawal.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I understand that the hon. member who has the floor

the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate-when I questioned his intention in the use of the word "dishonesty" indicated that he did not intend to impute dishonesty to any hon. member.
No sir. I said that I did not think the Prime Minister knows the facts. I think that if the Prime Minister had known the facts he would never have made that speech.
Withdraw.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps the matter would be very simply disposed of if the hon. member would say specifically that he withdraws the word "dishonest".

I withdraw unequivocally any imputation of dishonesty which I may have made to the Prime Minister or to any other member of this house. I did not say at any time, and I certainly did not intend to say at any time, that the Prime Minister deliberately distorted the facts. But I do say that when the facts such as I have put before the house now are presented in the fashion they were presented in the broadcast, the picture they gave is not a picture of the facts as, in fact, they are.
There is one other thing I should like to draw to the attention of the house in the very few minutes that remain. I refer to some remarks of the Prime Minister made, this time, as leader of the Progressive Conservative party at a testimonial dinner given by the Progressive Conservative associations of the Montreal area in his honour on May 8, 1959. Perhaps the exuberance of this expression may be partly explained by the nature of the occasion but it is, I think, an index of the sense of reality which characterizes everything done by this government that the Prime Minister's words, as reported in an official release from his own office, should have been as follows:
I have no hesitation in asserting at this time that I believe the government has accomplished more in these two years-
[Mr. Diefenbaker.!

That is, the two years they had been in office; it was not quite two years but it was close enough.
-than any other government in any time in our history. The tacts are on the record.
And then-I wonder this did not choke in the Prime Minister's throat:
One of the faults of our party when it has been in office is to take its good works too much for granted.
If ever a Prime Minister in the whole history of this country has boasted about the things which have been done, the things that might be done or the things that someone ought to get done but which never seemed to get done, it has been the present Prime Minister. Naturally, the question arises as to what this country would contribute to western defence if both of these programs were cancelled. I suggest that there is a vitally important and much more economical role for a middle power such as this country. That role lies in the provision of conventional forces to be available for possible action by the United Nations, and to fill the growing breach between peace and nuclear catastrophe. With the major powers concentrating more and more on the development of mammoth-powered, high-cost, nuclear weapons, the need for conventional forces is rapidly developing, forces which could meet a local conflict without setting off the final destruction of the world. We could join other middle non-nuclear powers in filling that role. We could equip our army, air force and navy with the best of conventional weapons and do the research for such a program. We could develop and manufacture this type of weapon in Canada for the use, not only of our own forces but also the forces of other middle powers. In doing so we could make an infinitely more valuable contribution to western defence and even world peace than we are now with our pair of Bomarc pea-shooters.
