I say to the minister that this type of rebuttal is a left-handed slap to the many people whose votes in the last election campaign gave his party the huge majority it now enjoys in this house today.
On his second appearance this afternoon, the Minister of Agriculture has still not given us any answers. The producers of eggs and hogs claim, and rightly so, that the legislation as it applies to eggs and hogs does not do what the government said it would do, namely that it would assist the industry of agriculture to realize fair returns for its labour and investment and to maintain a fair relationship between prices received by farmers and the cost of goods and services which they buy, thus providing farmers with a fair share of the national income.
This legislation was bailed by the government as the greatest ever. Listen to what the minister of northern affairs said during the last election campaign, as reported in the Regina Leader-Post of March 22,	1958,
when the minister spoke at Glenavon. This


article is headed, "Stabilization bill termed best ever", and this is what the minister had to say:
Speaking to farmers and businessmen, who in spite of snow blocked roads filled the Glenavon memorial hall to capacity, Mr. Hamilton said an example of the help the Tories would give to agriculture is the agricultural prices stabilization act which he described as "the best bill for the farmer that has ever been passed."
Again, the minister of northern affairs spoke in Wolseley, Saskatchewan, as reported in the Regina Leader-Post of March 21, 1958. He is reported to have said:
This bill will provide prices that will do more to give the farmer peace of mind, and enable him to operate more efficiently, than anything done to date in Canada's history.
In the same speech he said:
Let's get moving on the big things. Let western Canada give a western leader their support. John Diefenbaker is trusted by all people. He will not betray the trust.
I wonder, Mr. Speaker, what peace of mind the hog and egg producers have today? How much do they trust this government? Their feelings, I am confident, were expressed in clear and precise language the other day by the hon. member for Rosthern, (Mr. Nasser-den), a supporter of this government. This is what he said, as reported on page 470 of Hansard for January 28 last:
If I understand this program correctly, it is the most retrograde step that could be taken from an already established position. Moreover the arguments used are unworthy of an informed ministry.
These are words from a person who should know-a person representing an agricultural riding-in answer to the charge made by the Minister of Agriculture that the opposition did not know what it was talking about. What has happened to this great party which before the last election was asking the people of Canada to send Tories to Ottawa, men who knew the problems of the constituency and to whom people could look for advice? What does the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) think now of the hon. member for Rosthern who lined up with the Liberals and the C.C.F. in denouncing this policy of the government? I would like to remind the hon. gentleman of the statement he made in Wolseley, Saskatchewan in the course of the same speech which I quoted a moment ago. Listen to this:
Mr. Hamilton took the C.C.F. and Liberal Walter Tucker to task for having joined forces at Ottawa to misrepresent the agricultural prices stabilization bill. "Whenever you see Tucker and the C.C.F. getting friendly, run for the bushes," he told the laughing audience.
The hon. member for Rosthern who replaced Mr. Tucker is now lining up with the

Liberals and C.C.F. Who is laughing now, and who is running for the bushes? I wonder what would happen today if the minister of northern affairs and the Minister of Agriculture were to go out to Saskatchewan and repeat the statements they made during the last election campaign? I am sure they would get a crowd all right, snow blocked roads or not, but I would be willing to wager that the people who attended would not be armed with smiling faces but with eggs. Yes, Mr. Speaker, eggs, eggs that might just as well be used for decorating ministers as for selling at the prices received today.
Not as bad as the one you are laying.
We have had the latest speech from the hon. member for-where is it?
You wouldn't know.

Today is the ninth day we have spent on the speech from the throne, yet to date we have received very little by way of answers to questions raised on this side of the house. The reason, I submit, is that the government does not know the answers, has no laid down policy on anything, and waits until a crisis develops before making a decision.
I should like now to deal with matters concerning the people of my riding. The speech from the throne has two paragraphs dealing with the north. The first is as follows- I am quoting from Hansard for Thursday, January 14, page 2:
My government is pleased that its national development program has stimulated a large increase in northern exploration. Last year's discovery of oil and gas in the Yukon is being followed this year by a score of new exploratory wells over a wide area of northern Canada. Coupled with a revival of mining activity, this makes it evident that private enterprise is now active in the opening up of the north. New oil and gas regulations will emphasize opportunities for Canadians to participate in the ownership of these northern resources.
The government is implying that its national development policy has stimulated a large increase in northern exploration and that, as a result oil and gas were found in the Yukon. But what has this government done to expect any credit for the oil and gas found in the Eagle plain or Peel plateau area? Absolutely nothing. The companies finding this oil and gas have been working in this area since 1952 on a concession given to them by the former administration. A great deal of work has been done by these companies since that time, but the interest in this area began in 1957. As proof of this I call as witness the present minister of northern affairs who, speaking of the rush for oil permits in the Peel and Eagle plain
The Address-Mr. Hardie plateau area, as recorded on page 22 of the report of the standing committee on mines, forests and waters for Monday June 9, 1958, said:
The rush started last summer when word got out that this company was drilling. There was some staking last summer. Whether it started in June or not is not the point. It was completely separate and apart from government policy.
The government says now that its own national development program has been responsible for stimulating a large increase in further exploration. That is not true. The real reason is that the company which has been doing this work since 1952 hit oil and gas in a well which it was drilling during the past summer. Naturally this has sparked more interest in the area. As the minister said in 1958, the increased interest in the area was due to the work of the company and the same holds true today, if not more so. I hope the minister will not try to tell us the road from Flat Creek is what stimulated this interest, because he knows as well as I do that this road will not be of any help to the present permit holders who are required by regulation to do work to keep their permits in good standing. This road will not be completed in that area before the time limit of these permits expires.
There is also the interest taken in the area north of the British Columbia border and in the Northwest Territories. This was also due to the work done by the oil and gas companies. I could give another quotation from the minister in support of this statement, but I see that my time is running out, so I will not do so. In any event, this interest just above the British Columbia border on the Northwest Territories side was sparked by a find of gas last year, and resulted in the government selling rights to a considerable acreage. I understand that gas had been hit in that area recently and I expect that as this news becomes more widely known oil and gas companies will seek to get acreage in that area.
As far as the applications for permits in the Arctic islands is concerned, any interest in this area was due to the report of a survey carried out by the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys in 1955. These surveys are continuing, and if the reports show that the geological formation of the Arctic islands indicates that there are areas where oil and gas may be found, private oil and gas companies will naturally investigate.
Let us not hear any more of this malarkey from the minister that he and his policies have in the last year and a half made it possible for oil companies to find gas and oil. One would think from some of the articles and press reports written that he put the oil
536	HOUSE OF
The Address-Hon. D. M. Fleming and gas in the ground. As far as the mention in the speech from the throne concerning new gas and oil regulations is concerned- the promise that new regulations will be introduced by the government this year-I wonder if we can depend on this announcement any more than we could on the announcement made by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources on June 1 of last year to the committee on mines, forests and waters, when he stated that he expected these regulations to be approved by the cabinet during the first week of June of that year.
I submit that the real reason why the government has delayed bringing in the new regulations for so long has been to give an opportunity to a number of speculators who were able to obtain from the government applications for leases on millions of acres of ground, to sell acreage to companies who have the capital to do the work. We have heard a great deal lately from the minister in regard to low cost oil. Is this practice of allowing speculators to hold millions of acres on applications for permit with the sole intention of having oil companies pay through the nose for these rights giving us low cost oil?
When I read some of the statements the minister has made in regard to oil or gas finds in the north, he reminds me of a gypo stock promoter. The speech from the throne indicates that there has been a revival of mining in the north. Surely the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources is not going to tell us that he has made any changes in policy or in mining regulations or built any development roads. There has not been a new find in the Mackenzie district, Northwest Territories, since 1948 with the exception of Ray Rock which closed down last June nor has there been any mineral discovery since that made by the International Nickel Company.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as this ninth day of the present debate draws to a close may I hope it is not too late for one to extend his very sincere congratulations to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne for their most gracious speeches in opening this debate.
We are approaching the test in this house tonight of the confidence that the house has in the government. The opposition has challenged the confidence of the house. The debate has had a good many features to it.
I suppose I may be forgiven for turning back
[Mr. Hardie.l

to one of the earlier ones, the speech of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson).
It was on January 18 that he delivered his long, laboured, bitter and critical speech. In his view nothing that the government had done was right, everything was -wrong. He singled out in particular five spheres of government policy and administration for special criticism. They were defence, agriculture, trade, employment and finance. It did not take the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) very long to demolish that speech and attack and the Prime Minister indicated at the time that the ministers associated with four departments would in the course of this debate make statements. My colleagues the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness), the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) have already spoken and so far as I am able to do so I should like to make a statement to the house tonight in reply to the Leader of the Opposition concerning financial policy and administration.
The house will recall the scene on January 18. The stage was set. We were to see the new Pearson, the new man, the fighting tough man coming out of his corner slugging, taking on all comers. I welcome the Leader of the Opposition to his seat, Mr. Speaker, and I will repeat that sentence. On January 18 the stage was carefully set, painstakingly planned of course by the advisers of the Leader of the Opposition. We were to see the new Pearson, the new man, the tough fighting man coming out of his corner slugging, taking on all comers, rough, tough Lester.
The speech was to be replete with stinging accusations and harsh words. Why even the press releases were all prepared so that the headline material would be available to the press even before the speech had been completed. The headlines, of course, were to proclaim the speech a triumph. The Prime Minister was not even going to be given a chance to make his speech in the afternoon session.
Where were the headlines? There were no headlines for that speech of the Leader of the Opposition. They went, as we all well know, to the Prime Minister on his speech. But what I wish to draw attention to is the reaction of the Leader of the Opposition, the personal pique, the irritation, the choler that he demonstrated in the house and later in the week on the television program, plainly showing his personal irritation that he had been deprived of the triumph that was to be his.
There are so many things in the speech of the hon. gentleman that invite answer that I am going to have to proceed very quickly. Let me say in summary that I believe it is one of

the most misleading and irresponsible speeches ever delivered in the House of Commons. I am not taking time to dwell on the fact that it was full of sneers, snide remarks and superficialities, but I do wish to say something about the errors, the half-truths, quarter-truths and untruths that found their way into that speech.
Here let me deal as briefly as I can with just a few. I have picked out about 20 and I do not know if I will have time to go beyond that. Number one; turning to page 49 of Hansard of January 18 we find the hon. gentleman saying:
-in the cold and objective language of the report of the dominion bureau of statistics in the statistical review which came out a few weeks ago recovery and expansion have been less vigorous in Canada than in the United States.
In fact this is what that issue did say:
It must always be borne in mind that as the recession, itself, was mild in Canada, so the recovery and expansion has been less vigorous than in the United States. However, by the second quarter of 1959, the rate of expansion in relation to previous peaks was about the same in the two countries.
Number two; on page 49 the hon. gentleman said:
-the bureau indicated an increase in our gross national product during the year of 5 per cent in volume. To get it into perspective I should point out that in 1955-another year of economic recovery -the increase in the gross national product was 8.5 per cent and in 1956, 8.6 per cent.
The fact is that in the dominion bureau of statistics third quarter national accounts in which the D.B.S. mentioned the volume increase of 5 per cent they put it into perspective by saying this:
-this compares with... a postwar average for the years 1947 to 1958 of 4 per cent per year.
So you see, Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman's perspective was just a little cast in the shade there. Number three; at page 49 the hon. gentleman said:
I should also point out that there has been no increase-
Here he is speaking of the gross national product. I continue:
-in the third quarter of 1959, so it is a little premature to say that the battle has been spectacularly won.
The fact is that the dominion bureau of statistics in its third quarter national accounts points out the factors which contributed to a slowdown in the third quarter. Here are its words in that respect:
1. Of some importance in this country was the strike of 27,000 forestry workers in British Columbia which had a major impact on production and income in both forestry and in durable goods manufacturing.
The Address-Hon. D. M. Fleming
2. The repercussions of the (steel) strike on the United States economy have probably influenced climate and course of the business expansion in Canada.
Number four; at page 49 this is what we heard from the hon. gentleman on the question of unemployment:
The fact is that the average-
He was speaking of unemployment. I continue:
-is 348,000 and it is going up. These 348,000 unemployed are more than in the United States.
What are the facts now? If one takes account of the seasonal factors one might say that perhaps one third to two fifths of the total unemployment in this country is seasonal, and this is evident by our average levels in comparison with other countries. Despite this fact, our average is no higher than that of the United States, the hon. gentleman to the contrary notwithstanding. The rate in Canada for the 11 months for which the figures are complete has been running at 5.6 per cent. That percentage is almost identical with that of the United States. The United States total unemployment in December was 3,577,000.
Number five; the hon. gentleman said that the municipalities are finding it more and more difficult to raise the money to meet their own share-page 49. What are the facts? Mr. Speaker, if the house will give me permission to put a table on Hansard, I may say to you that it will show very clearly the municipalities are doing better in this respect than they did in the periods spoken of by the hon. gentleman. May I have leave of the house, Mr. Speaker, to put this table on the record?
Could the minister tell us what the table is?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A table of municipal borrowings from the year 1956 to the end of nine months of 1959, inclusive.
Can the minister indicate what the origin of the figures is?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Department of Finance, from government sources.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Has the minister leave to incorporate the table in Hansard?
Agreed.

Can the minister say
whether these figures have been published previously?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, I think they are all available in public form. They go up to the end of nine months of 1959, the last date for which those figures are complete. They will show that whereas at the end of

The Address-Hon. D. M. Fleming 1956 outstanding bank loans of municipalities amounted to $117 million, at the end of the first nine months of 1959 they amounted to $227 million, and in terms of gross new issues delivered in 1956, bond issues, for the full year the total was $358 million. For the first nine months alone of 1959 the total was $338 million. Therefore, the facts are all against the Leader of the Opposition.

Will the minister give the average rate of interest?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: At page 50, the Leader of the Opposition-
Will the minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am sorry; I will not have time for questions unless the hon. gentleman would like to ask them at the conclusion of my remarks. I shall be glad to answer any questions then. Number six, at page 50 the Leader of the Opposition says this:
Anyway, perhaps the minister has read this article by a man who certainly cannot be accused of any political affiliation or political or party prejudice. I refer to the article by Professor Neufeld in the Canadian Banker last autumn, and he is a real authority on the subject. Professor Neufeld said, and I am going to quote from page 663.
Then, he proceeded to quote from that page concerning an upward move in interest rates. I have looked into this. The article referred to did not appear in the Canadian Banker but in an English publication called The Banker. The quotation in Hansard is correct, but Professor Neufeld also had the following to say:
Events in the Canadian capital market in recent months have prompted some observers to talk with exaggeration of a "credit crisis".
This is an expression the Leader of the Opposition has used. You know, Professor Neufeld also said this before the quotation read into the record by the Leader of the Opposition:


Since that time-that is, late in 1958-the money supply has remained virtually constant: the government has had to finance its deficit by selling short term issues at prices demanded by the market. The final indication that this policy of competing for funds was not only the correct one but also a practicable one came last September when several new government issues sold well. While there is no doubt that the government will have to raise further money, it at least now has a firmer bond market in which to seek its funds. This improved market tone, together with the possibility that the government net cash requirements from the market may disappear in the first half of 1960, has made the problem of selling government issues considerably more attractive than it seemed a short while ago.
Before I leave the subject, it is worthy of note, I think, that Professor Neufeld says that the market determines the price and interest rates of short term issues, not as the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition would have led one to believe, that the government determines those interest rates. Mr. Speaker, it goes on and on.
Number seven; at page 50 the Leader of the Opposition says:
This monetary crisis, because it certainly was that as the minister will admit-
He refers to the Minister of Finance, Mr. Speaker. Let me say to him that the minister does not admit false and untrue statements of that kind. There has not been a monetary crisis. This country is in a very solid and sound financial condition and has been throughout this period.
Number eight; at page 51 the Leader of the Opposition said:
The government's decision to expand the money supply-
He is speaking about 1958. That was not a government decision; that was a decision taken by the Bank of Canada.
Nonsense.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: What did you say in 1956?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Here is what goes on. The testimony continued:
I think myself that the Bank of Canada Act is in this respect a very good act, and better than most, because it is clear. There is no alibi possible for the central bank.
On the other hand, there is no alibi possible for the government-
And here is where the Leader of the Opposition picks out his statement:
-because if government said:	well, we disagreed with what the central bank did, but parliament has placed the responsibility on them, so what could we do? The answer obviously is that the administration of the day, supported by a majority in parliament, can always alter the legislation.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that the Leader of the Opposition gave a very misleading interpretation of what was said by Mr. Graham Towers in his testimony.
Read page 51.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I come to number 10. On page 52, the Leader of the Opposition purports to quote the Prime Minister as saying:
In the fall of 1958, we increased the money supply by 12 per cent.
If he will be fair with the Prime Minister he will know that the Prime Minister when he spoke that way was not referring to the government but to Canada.
Number 11; at page 52 the hon. gentleman was referring to the Prime Minister, and he said:
He said then that there had been no freezing of the money supply by the government.
Yes, certainly, there had been no freezing of the money supply, because the government is not freezing the money supply. Only the Bank of Canada has power over the volume of currency in circulation.
That is the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If the hon. member wants the law amended let him and his
The Address-Hon. D. M. Fleming party come out from under cover where they have been hiding and say so.
Number 12; at page 52 the Leader of the Opposition says:
We have had in the past much greater demand for funds for much greater expansion under Liberal administration without such high interest rates and with less scarcity of funds. Let the Minister of Finance deny that statement if he can.
Let me put the facts squarely on the record. There was a greater demand for funds in the form of bank commercial credit in the period from the middle of 1958 to the summer of 1959, than there had been in any comparable period previous to that time in Canada's history. There is the fact.
Because of your $2 billion of borrowing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not because of our borrowing, Mr. Speaker.
You were sopping it all up.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We will come to that matter of borrowing if hon. gentlemen opposite can possess their souls in patience.
Number 13; as found on page 52 the Leader of the Opposition said that we had "$2 billion cash deficits in two years." We did not have $2 billion cash deficits in two years. If he knew what he was talking about when he referred to cash deficits he would have known, whether he was talking about fiscal years or whether he was talking about calendar years, that total cash deficits amounted not to $2 billion but to $1J billion. But he does not like fractions so $1J billion is the same thing as $2 billion to him. What is $500 million to him?
The next one is Number 14, I believe. I am losing track of these numbers. As found on page 53 he said of the government of which he was a member:
-we did put into effect monetary restrictions in a period of boom.
That is not true. It was the Bank of Canada that put into effect the monetary restrictions at the time to which he refers. So one can go on, Mr. Speaker.
The next one I have must be Number 15. As found on page 54 he said:
-in the last two years of his financial administration fiscal policy has not been flexible.
He is completely wrong there because the distinguishing feature of government fiscal policy in the last two and a half years has been its flexibility. We adapted it each time to the changing conditions and just as fast as conditions of parliamentary government with an annual budget would permit.

The Address-Hon. D. M. Fleming
Let us take the next one, Number 16. As found on page 60 the Leader of the Opposition said:
-the figure for our deficit in international payments for the first nine months of 1959 was $919 million. This, of course, is profoundly disturbing-
Yes, he told the truth, Mr. Speaker. In the first nine months of 1959 the deficit with the United States was indeed $919 million, but in the last full year of Liberal administration the deficit with the United States for the first nine months of 1956 was $1,204 million. Apparently that was not so disturbing.
You said you were going to correct it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Number 17, again on page 60, the Leader of the Opposition said:
As the dominion bureau of statistics points out, -nearly 29 per cent-
He was speaking of the unfavourable balance.
-is now financed by inflows of other character, mostly of a short term character.
The dominion bureau of statistics publication, Canada's Balance of International Payments, third quarter, 1959, states:
In the third quarter some types of short term inflow continued, particularly in the earlier part of the period, but there were also outflows offsetting most of this group of inflows.
Number 18; on page 60 the Leader of the Opposition said:
Of this inflow of capital, 80 per cent is now coming from the United States and only 5 per cent from the United Kingdom, though in the preceding year, 1958, that figure was 15 per cent. There is a change in the wrong direction.
What are the facts? The statement of the Leader of the Opposition gives the impression, of course, that the United States figure is increasing while the United Kingdom figure is decreasing. The D.B.S. third quarter International Balance of Payments publication says:
Geographically slightly more than 80 per cent of the capital inflows in long term forms during the first nine months have come from the United States. This was also the experience in 1958. Net inflows from the United Kingdom represented less than 5 per cent of the movement in 1959 compared with about 15 per cent in 1958. A considerable part of the change reflected outflows from Canada for direct investment in the United Kingdom, although the completion in 1958 of repayments by the United Kingdom on the $700 million loan of 1942 was also an important factor-
One is left to wonder in the face of this fact whether the Leader of the Opposition is concerned about our investing in the United Kingdom or is lamenting the end of the repayments to Canada on the loan we made to the United Kingdom some years ago.
That is a diversion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Number 19, page 61, and this is a fine example of trickery with words, the Leader of the Opposition said:
We have a merchandise deficit with the United States of $609 million. Last year for the same 11-month period we had a merchandise deficit of $288 million, so that has gone up and that is profoundly disturbing. Indeed, one of the things from which the government took the greatest satisfaction last year during a period of strong recession was the fact we had cut down our adverse balance of trade with the United States. Well, it has now gone up to $609 million.
Note these words, "It has gone up to $609 million". The fact is that the deficit with the United States for 11 months this year was, as the Leader of the Opposition said, $609 million. The total deficit with all countries for the first 11 months of 1958, as he said, was $288 million. But the deficit with the United States for the first 11 months of 1958 was $643 million. Thus the United States deficit has decreased this year and not increased unless decrease means to the Leader of the Opposition to go up. The fact is that it went down from $643 million to $609 million whereas the Leader of the Opposition says it has now gone up to $609 million.
Number 20, page 61, the Leader of the Opposition said:
Of those increased imports 14.5 per cent came from the United Kingdom. How much came from the United States? Of this increase in imports, 56.2 per cent came from the United States. '
What are the facts? This, of course, left the impression that we were increasing our share of imports from the United States. For the first 11 months of 1959 we increased the share of our imports from the United Kingdom, from other commonwealth countries and from other areas. The share of our imports coming from the United States decreased from 68.9 per cent to 67.8 per cent. In 1956, the last full year of Liberal rule, the share of our imports coming from the United States was 73 per cent.
I wish there were time, to dwell on more of these palpable errors, half-truths, quarter-truths and untruths in the speech of the Leader of the Opposition but time does not permit. I wish to deal now with something that I think is worthy of comment in the Canadian House of Commons. I refer to the sedulous, persistent efforts made by the Leader of the Opposition to destroy confidence. I do not mind if in partisan warfare the Leader of the Opposition wishes to do what he can to destroy confidence in the government. That is perfectly lawful and proper in a democracy, if that is the tactic that he chooses.
But, Mr. Speaker, when the Leader of the Opposition chooses at the same time to destroy confidence in Canada that is a very

different matter as far as we are concerned. In this respect I say that the Leader of the Opposition has followed a reckless and irresponsible course. Need I remind you, sir, of the things that he said last year? Here is a statement by him as found on page 40 of Hansard of last year. I have selected three sentences on that page:
-there is now decreasing confidence in the country, in the stability of our dollar, and this means danger. ... At the end of ... 1958 the Canadian investing public held less government bonds than at the beginning, $7,953 million as against $8,628 million. . .. The integrity of Canada's credit has never been questioned before as it is being questioned now.
That was not said by some external enemy of Canada; that was said in this house by the Leader of the Opposition.
Shame.
That is pretty cheap stuff.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In the same speech, page 41, he talked about reaching a "crisis of confidence", with rising prices, rising costs, rising deficits and, along with these, rising unemployment. That was the picture that he sought to paint of Canada in 1959. We well remember the way he gloried in gloom, the way he went about the country prophesying a deficit of over $1 billion. When the final figure was made known I am sure it was very disappointing to him to find that the deficit was only $609 million. He had taken the actual amount, you see, and just added the usual Liberal two thirds to it for good measure. And they are not through with this tactic yet.
Hon. members who listened to the speech by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Che-vrier) in this house last Thursday night will have observed that the hon. gentleman announced with great emphasis that the deficit last year was $862 million. He is just $253 million over the fact. That is, of course, I suppose the measure of leeway that has to be extended to those who make use of the Martin bureau of statistics. When they take figures and facts and apply surgery to them we well now know that it is manipulative surgery that they apply.
That was in the throne speech debate a year ago. But the Leader of the Opposition was not satisfied with the claim that he made then. When he came to take part in the budget debate last year you will find some of the comments he had to make on April 21 of that year at page 2912 of Hansard, when he addressed the Minister of Finance as follows:
I tell him and the government that the word of Canada-
Mark this, Mr. Speaker.
-does not mean as much now as it did.
The Address-Hon. D. M. Fleming
It is true, too.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If ever a member in this house made a statement that will redound to his shame as long as he stays in this house it was that statement, and it will redound to the everlasting shame of the hon. gentleman who uttered it. This is the Leader of the Opposition saying to the world, saying to anybody who will listen to him that there is something wrong with the good name of Canada when Canada puts her name to obligations-
Ask any egg producer or any hog producer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
He was talking about confidence in Canada, both at home and abroad. I will say to him that no one has done more, in the way he has gone about his partisan tasks, to weaken confidence in Canada, both at home and abroad, than he has.
Then the Leader of the Opposition went on to deal with my forecast of a 7 per cent increase in the gross national product. He said that was far too optimistic a forecast and it had been dismissed by many experts. He had to admit himself in speaking in this house two weeks ago that the forecast of the Minister of Finance was not too optimistic and the figure forecast has been equalled with a 7 per cent increase in the gross national product.
In the throne speech debate this year he has some interesting things to say. At page 50 he announces we are still in a condition of recession. At page 49 he talks about the boom. He does not admit we are in a boom, he simply says we are acquiring some of the worst monetary evils of a boom. You see, signs of improvement hurt him; nothing is right, so he pursues his petty, unrealistic, carping course. He had something to say about deficits, but on January 19, 1959, he had a different tune about deficits. He said the previous administration did not hesitate to budget for a deficit when there was a threat of recession. What did we do? We budgeted
602	HOUSE OF
The Address-Hon. D. M. Fleming for a deficit when there was a recession. In 1958 we were meeting the problems of a recession, then at its low point, and were seeking to use fiscal measures to offset the decline in business activity and to stimulate recovery. We gave strong support to new housing construction; we increased substantially our own direct expenditures on capital projects; we reduced our own resources to increase those of the provinces and municipalities; we sustained and enlarged the general purchasing power of the Canadian public, both by tax reductions and increases in pensions and other welfare payments.
In 1959, one year ago, we were budgeting for a period of recovery. Our problem was to strike a balance. It was not yet a time for a severe application of fiscal restraint, but the situation did require a reduction in the stimulus which government fiscal policies had injected into the economic stream. We took a firm course designed to ward off the perils of inflation and to preserve the purchasing power of the Canadian dollar without retarding the forces of recovery, and we have succeeded.
Could the minister say from what he was quoting?

I must conclude now, and I do so on this matter of confidence. Surely, Mr. Speaker, the real test of confidence in Canada's word, Canada's credit, is the way people buy Canadian securities, and here are the facts. The return to public confidence has been striking. The public's willingness to purchase government bonds is, in the last analysis, the best test of its confidence. In 1955 the general public's holdings of government of Canada securities were about $9 billion; by mid-1958 they had fallen to less than $8 billion; today the public's holdings of our bonds exceed $10,750 million, an increase of $2,750 million in fifteen months. Mr. Speaker, due to circumstances beyond my control I feel tonight that I have to cut my speech to the bare minimum. Accordingly I will dispense with the normal courtesies at this time and restrict my speech to the main tenor of my remarks.
I should like to deal tonight with a subject that has been very carefully avoided by the government so far, with exception of the minister who took his seat just now, who mentioned it in passing. I refer to the problem of social security in this country. In order to deal properly with the problem of social security we should first have a definition of what it is. One of the best I have seen is the one in the universal declaration of human rights, adopted on December 10, 1948 by the general assembly of the United Nations. It appears in article 25 and is as follows:
Everyone has the right to ... security in the event of unemployment, sickness, disability, widowhood, old age or other lack of livelihood in circumstances beyond his control.
I should also like to go back as far as 1911 to Charles W. Eliot, president of Harvard University.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: TABLE 2 AVERAGE TERM TO MATURITY OF UNMATURED MARKETABLE GOVERNMENT ISSUES
speechtext: Order. I would request a little more attention from the house. It is difficult to hear the hon. member who has the floor.

maintopic: TABLE 2 AVERAGE TERM TO MATURITY OF UNMATURED MARKETABLE GOVERNMENT ISSUES
speechtext:
Mr. Eliot put it in this way:
A declaration of independence if it were written now, would among other things set forth that every citizen in a free state has an inalienable right to that amount of employment which will yield for him and his family a decent living: that every worker has a right to be insured against the personal losses due to acute sickness, chronic invalidism, injuries through accident, and the inevitable disabilities of old age.
As social security has developed over the years in various countries it has generally taken three forms. They are social insurance, such as workmen's compensation and unemployment insurance; public service, such as old age pensions and family pensions, to mention the two most prominent; and social assistance, such as old age assistance, blind pensions, mothers allowances, and many others. In addition to that there is any number of social services such as workmen's compensation for industrial accidents, industrial sickness, pensions, life insurance, group insurance, funeral benefits, bonuses, holiday pay, vacation pay, and many others.

Also, of course, there is a matter of medical care. Doctor Rosenfeld, the associate executive director of the community health association of Detroit, Michigan, describes medical care in this way:
The need for medical care may be described in terms of those services which in accordance with current medical concepts are required by the individual and the family to prevent illness, disability and death; to ameliorate pain and anxiety, and to assist the individual and the family to realize their maximum potentialities-biological, psychological and social.
It might also be opportune at this time just to look back and see just how social security has developed over the years. It goes back even to primitive tribes, when the tribes used to look after their own. From there it developed to private and religious charity. Then through the middle ages there were the guilds which helped in some way to look after their fellow men. The great depression of the thirties gave it a great stimulus and pointed to the need of much greater assistance than before; and the advent of world war II saw the development of the trade unions in this country who, when wages were frozen, proceeded to get fringe benefits incorporated into contracts and thus alleviate various hardships. There is one great weakness with this form and that is that while these fringe benefits are written in the contracts, it means that everyone is paying and only a few are benefiting.
Urbanization and industrialization forced the general public to believe that democratic government has a responsibility to its citizens. Doctor Altmeyer, former United States commissioner of social security, speaking to the Canadian Labour Congress on December 1 of last year, quoted no less a person than the former prime minister of Great Britain, Sir Winston Churchill. This again goes right back to 1911 when Mr. Churchill was at that time a member of the Liberal party in Great Britain and was responsible for the development of the famous Beveridge plan. He had this to say:
I do not agree with those who say that every man must look after himself and that the intervention of the state will be fatal to his self-reliance, to his foresight and his thrift. If terror be an incentive to thrift, surely the penalties of the system which we have abandoned ought to have stimulated thrift as much as anything else could have been stimulated in this world. The mass of the labouring people have known that unless they made provision for their old age betimes, they would perish miserably in the workhouse.
We have seen social security develop in other countries such as Great Britain, Sweden, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, and even in the U.S.S.R. where pensions are now being related to past earnings. However, one

thing I would like to make very clear. Freedom and security are synonymous. You cannot have one without the other. Another thing we should also keep in mind is that social security should provide a safety net and not a feather bed.
What is our present position in this country with regard to social security? The same Doctor Altmeyer had this to say, and I think his words are very wise:
Certainly one great lesson that countries have learned the hard way is that it is vitally necessary to plan and develop a long-range, unified, harmonious and balanced system in order to avoid gaps, duplications and anomalies. They have found that unless they do it is impossible to achieve the goal of providing maximum security at a minimum cost. Unfortunately in many countries specific needs and demands have been considered only as they happened to attract public attention. As a result action has been taken on specific measures separately and independently. The result has been that in the course of time an unplanned, chaotic, inefficient and costly conglomeration of measures has come into existence. Vested interests in the continuance of each separate measure cause great difficulties in the development of a rational social security program.
That, I would say, is a very good picture of what we have in Canada at the present time. We find at the present time, to use one small illustration, that we are squandering far too much of our medical dollar on institutional care. The reason for this is that with regard to health in this country we are flying on one wing. We have, after long delay, introduced a system of hospital insurance across Canada, yet what do we find? We find cases where doctors have to order their patients into hospital even though they could be treated just as well, and perhaps better, inside their own homes. Doctors do this because they know that patients cannot afford treatment outside hospitals. One might almost say that hospitals are being used as hotels. Certainly, they are the most expensive hotels one could find in the country. Mr. Altmeyer also has this to say:
Although the voluntary plans are attempting to cleave to the principle of community rating, this position will be difficult for them to maintain in the face of competition with insurance companies. Medical care insurance would not seem to provide an appropriate area for the free play of the competitive practices that are acceptable in commerce. It is an area in which governmental regulation would seem to be not only appropriate-but necessary.
The hodgepodge of various plans that we have across the country at the present time tends to raise the cost to all small groups; to women's groups, to older people and to those in dangerous occupations.
We have a multitude of plans both public and private. They are in certain cases very inefficient and, in most cases, they are certainly duplicating costs. They are confusing to us at home and they are overwhelming to
The Address-Mr. M. W. Martin visitors coming to this country. Such various and endless types of plan seem very impressive, but unfortunately far too many of our citizens find themselves being led into a sense of false security; when they come to use a particular plan which they think covers them, they find to their surprise that they are not covered in the way they thought they were. Another danger which has grown up as a result of this multitude of plans was pointed out by Mr. J. S. Morgan, professor of social work at the University of Toronto, in a passage of a recent book about Great Britain. Professor Morgan wrote:
So far, two stages in the development of the corporate finance of privilege can be discerned. First there is the use of corporate funds to supplement management incomes, to compensate the chosen for the tax encroachments of the state. There are many forms such aid can take; the provision of pensions, cars, expense allowances, interest-free loans, etc. the shape being determined by the provisions of the tax code. But the second stage goes much further. The country house and the flat in town are owned by the corporation but used by the individual; the chauffeur, the butler and the gardener serve the individual but are now maintained on the company payroll. The corporation owns its own cars, its yacht, its country club, even its aeroplane; but all are used by its senior employees.
I would submit that this situation would not be foreign to Canada.
As nearly as we can find from the figures available, at least with the research facilities open to us, of all the medical bills of last year, with all this multitude of plans, only 27 per cent of the bills were covered by these plans. For example, it is estimated that the drug bill alone accounts for 25 cents of every medical dollar. It seems, also, that both past and present governments have been obsessed with trying to leave health care in the hands of life insurance companies. I notice in the papers the other night that the hon. member for Hamilton South (Mr. McDonald)-whether he was expressing the ideas of the government or not, I am not sure-advocated that the government should give up all the insurance field and leave it to the insurance companies.

In addition, the present costs of social security measures to the federal government are estimated to be $1,856,196,000. For example, the cost of old age pensions and family allowances comes to some $900 million. Figures available for eight of the ten provinces show that, in addition, the provinces spend some $170,523,637 in this field, ranging from a low in Nova Scotia of something over $5 million to a high in Quebec of nearly $68 million. in exchange for every dollar spent? I know it is very difficult to make an estimate but I would suggest that if we are getting 25 cents value for every dollar spent in this field it would be a generous estimate.

I would suggest that one of the reasons we are not getting much 
value for our money is because of the way we got into this social security program, stumbling blindly in the dark with no thought as to where we are going, how we are going to get there or what we want when we do get there. These programs have been brought about by world events and by political pressure at home. The government, unfortunately, has gone down the road of social security with both feet dragging and firmly braced. It sometimes seems that the government wants to prove itself right in delaying it so long. We have many gaps in our social security program. One of the main reasons is because far too many Canadians think that minimum standards and not minimum health and decency are what we are striving for.
I see that my time is getting short and I am going to have to by-pass some very important parts of this extremely significant

subject. I should like to go on now to consider just what we may hope to attain in the future and what will be needed then. The following are some of the questions I suggest we should ask ourselves. First, on what basis are, or should, family allowance rates be determined? Have we ever faced up to the situation? Since they were first inaugurated in 1945 have we considered what purchasing value they have today as compared to the purchasing value they had then?
Second, what grounds are there for different rates of benefit in the same circumstances of income need, depending upon whether the cause of need is a war injury, an industrial injury or disease, unemployment, desertion of the breadwinner, death of the breadwinner or sickness of the breadwinner? I do not want any misunderstanding about references made in this question to war injuries. I am a veteran myself and a war pensioner. I know that Canadian veterans have never asked the government for special favours. They have merely asked to be treated the same as people who did not have that time lapse in their normal lives.
Third, what grounds are there for differentiating the payments in respect of children in a family receiving aid as between the dependents of a recipient of unemployment insurance, the dependents of a sick breadwinner and the dependents of a veteran or a workman suffering industrial injury?
In the short time at my disposal I have tried to outline the magnitude of the job that lies before us. One of the things that has bothered me greatly, as I am sure it has anyone who has given any thought to this matter, is that far too many of the payments made under our social security systems-[DOT] and I say "systems" instead of "system" because that is exactly what we have-are based on law rather than on need. To qualify you have to meet certain standards. The payment, for example, may be $55 a month. There is no provision made in cases where the payment should be $45. Perhaps the need is for $100 but the law says so much and unfortunately that is what we have to accept at the present time. I say there is a big job ahead for the government in this field and certainly there is no need for smugness on its part when it considers the lack of an adequate program in this country. There is a staggering job to be done and I urge the government to get on with it.

In the light of subsequent information, this aspect of the matter is now under discussion between the two governments.
3.	Answered by 2 above.

1.	Has the Minister of Labour received a report from the Vocational Training Advisory Council respecting the vocational training program for unemployed persons under federal-provincial costsharing arrangements?
2.	What is being done by the federal government to encourage the fullest possible use of this program to provide new job opportunities for jobless persons with no formal training in a specific trade?
Questions
Answer by: Hon. Michael Starr (Minister of
Labour):
1.	This program was discussed at the last meeting of the vocational training advisory council held on December 3 and 4, 1959, and the views of the council, as recorded in the minutes of the meeting, have been received.
2.	The federal government is constantly urging provincial governments to make the greatest possible use of the federal-provincial cost-sharing program provided in schedule "M" of the special vocational training projects agreement for training of unemployed persons. A continuing program for training unemployed persons is in operation in the four western provinces and New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, as well as a number of courses in Ontario. During the present fiscal year 3,200 unemployed persons have been trained.
In addition to the continuing program, last winter a special program was set up for upgrading seasonally unemployed workers in Saskatchewan and is being repeated again this winter.
Alberta is establishing a similar program this winter in Edmonton.
Recently the unemployment insurance commission revised its program for referring unemployed persons to approved courses in private and public schools and the base of eligibility for unemployment insurance benefits while attending training programs was broadened.
Trade school facilities are being expanded in six provinces under our vocational and technical training agreement. These will make more training opportunities available for adult workers.
Question No. 85

1.	Is the Ontario government withholding sales tax on purchases by it and its crown corporations? If so, since when?
2.	What is the estimated amount to date of the Ontario sales tax holdback?
Answer by: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister
of National Revenue):
1.	The Excise Tax Act requires the Canadian manufacturer, i.e., vendor, to pay the tax and not the purchaser. Canadian manufacturers are permitted to sell goods, normally subject to tax, sales tax free to departments of the Ontario government where the goods are for use by the provincial department. Canadian manufacturers are required to pay sales tax on the sale of taxable goods to provincial crown corporations. It is not known whether or not these corporations are withholding payment of tax to their suppliers.
2.	Answered in 1, above.
